attempts.answer:
Below are continual learning strategies that let a scientific assistant decide when new literature should overwrite versus coexist with prior conclusions. We synthesize mechanisms across continual learning (CL), uncertainty and novelty detection, and retrieval-grounded QA, and map them to concrete policies for updating a scientific narrative.

# Core Problem and Decision Framing

Continual learning systems face a plasticity–stability trade‑off: too much plasticity causes catastrophic forgetting where new learning overwrites old; too much stability prevents learning new findings, leading to irrelevance and contradictions over time<cite id="0ff96ec3-4">Striking a balance between plasticity and stability is critical; too much plasticity leads to catastrophic forgetting where new learning overwrites past knowledge, while too much stability prevents learning new concepts</cite><cite id="0ff96ec3-1">LLMs underpinning AI Scientist systems suffer hallucinations and inefficient knowledge updating with catastrophic forgetting, where updating can overwrite prior concepts and facts</cite><cite id="0ff96ec3-2">Iterative fine-tuning can exhibit “palimpsest” behavior where new data overwrite prior knowledge, demonstrating catastrophic forgetting</cite>. For scientific assistants, the question becomes: when new evidence is (i) novel, (ii) contradicts prior claims, (iii) sufficiently uncertain/conflicted, or (iv) temporally/epistemologically superior, should the agent update (overwrite) or preserve parallel versions (coexist)?

# Algorithmic Building Blocks That Operationalize “Overwrite vs Coexist”

1) Uncertainty-aware updating and selective retraining
- Reliable uncertainty estimates are essential to decide whether current knowledge fits new data; methods like softmax probabilities, entropy/margin, temperature-scaled scores, Bayesian predictive uncertainty, and Mahalanobis distances inform continual novelty detection and active learning updates<cite id="490a4a6a-3">Uncertainty estimation (softmax, entropy/margin/softmax variants; Bayesian neural networks; Mahalanobis distance) is crucial; in CL, uncertainty quality degrades over time without continual integration, leading to poor novelty detection and sample selection unless addressed</cite><cite id="490a4a6a-2">Baselines for continual novelty detection use entropy/margin/softmax uncertainty to select uncertain samples and output scores; uncertainty metrics integrated into continual training updates</cite>. 
- Incorporating continual novelty detection into incremental pipelines (e.g., incDFM) enables the system to distinguish “in-distribution vs novel” and to trigger targeted updates rather than wholesale retraining, reducing overwrite risk for stable findings<cite id="490a4a6a-3">incDFM integrates continual novelty detection into unsupervised class incremental learning, enabling detection and integration of novel data rather than global retraining</cite><cite id="490a4a6a-1">COUQ provides uncertainty for continual novelty detection and active learning, showing utility across sub-tasks</cite>.
- Practical policy: if posterior uncertainty on a claim is below a threshold given new evidence, defer or merge; if uncertainty is high and evidence is consistent, update weights; if evidence is inconsistent, trigger conflict analysis rather than blanket overwrite<cite id="490a4a6a-3">Novelty and active learning depend on reliable uncertainty; poor uncertainty in CL leads to errors accumulating over time, motivating mechanisms that integrate new knowledge without full retraining</cite>.

2) Novelty and out-of-distribution detection at the stream level
- Novelty detection links directly to CL: separating “in” (previously/recently learned), “forgotten” (previously correct now misclassified due to drift), and “out” (novel) supports targeted integration; simple softmax-based detectors can be surprisingly robust, but distinguishing “forgotten” from “in” remains hard without continual integration mechanisms<cite id="0ff96ec3-0">Novelty detection links to CL; samples can be partitioned into In (previously/recently learned), Forged (forgotten/now mispredicted), and Out (novel); methods’ behaviors and errors change under continual updating</cite><cite id="0ff96ec3-4">Novelty detection methods can be grouped and evaluated on continual splits; performance degrades without continual integration</cite><cite id="490a4a6a-4">Continual novelty detection divides into In vs Out, In vs Forg, and Forg vs Out; detection error increases with continual learning, and simple softmax can work best yet poorly depending on settings</cite>.
- Policy implication: classify new literature as novel, redundant, or conflicting; if novel and sufficiently distinct, create a parallel record and schedule a later merge/evaluation; if forgotten/irrelevant, demote or discard; if overlapping and consistent, update confidence and summaries<cite id="0ff96ec3-4">Balancing plasticity and stability lets systems preserve old knowledge while integrating new; methods cluster into memory-, regularization-, and architecture-based families</cite>.

3) Self-correcting RAG pipelines and iterative retrieval
- Agentic RAG introduces iterative retrieval–reflection–refinement cycles for self-correction, enabling models to detect when additional evidence is needed and to revise prior answers; methods like Self-RAG, CRAG, FLARE, ActiveRAG, and RAG-Critic operationalize correction loops and error-aware decision-making over retrieval and generation<cite id="e93bc512-0">Agentic RAG (Self-RAG, CRAG, FLARE, ActiveRAG) iteratively retrieves and refines responses, enabling self-correction and improved factual accuracy in multi-document QA</cite><cite id="e93bc512-2">FLARE triggers retrieval based on generation-time uncertainty; ReSP iterates retrieve–summarize–plan; SIM-RAG and RAG-Critic train critics to accept answers or continue searching based on error taxonomies, enabling targeted correction</cite>.
- Quantitatively, retrieval augmentation reduces self-contradictions by ~30–50% but a notable fraction remains, indicating that contradictions often stem from irrelevant or missing evidence; this motivates policies that overwrite earlier claims when new evidence directly contradicts with high confidence, or coexist with annotations when confidence is moderate<cite id="e93bc512-1">Retrieval augmentation reduces self-contradictions by ~30% (ChatGPT) and ~50% (Llama2-70B) yet 12.7–38.0% of sentences remain contradictory with high precision; contradictions often arise from irrelevant or lacking crucial information</cite>.
- Policy implication: maintain a working answer with provenance and confidence; on new literature, run a quick sufficiency check: if evidence resolves gaps or contradicts with high confidence, update the claim and confidence; if only partially relevant or conflicted, produce a coexisting view with highlighted conflicts and a resolution plan<cite id="e93bc512-2">S2G-RAG formalizes structured sufficiency and gap judging, interleaving retrieval control to accept answers or continue searching based on evidence evaluation</cite>.

4) Evidence reranking for scientific accuracy and conflict mitigation
- Scientific assistants risk absorbing semantically similar yet logically irrelevant passages; deep evidence reranking with agentic reasoning explicitly models logical relevance and evidential support, filtering misleading evidence before fusion into answers<cite id="e93bc512-4">DeepEra introduces an agentic deep evidence reranking agent that models logical relevance and evidential support to address vulnerabilities of surface-level rerankers and the lack of explicit reranking in agent-based scientific QA</cite>.
- Policy implication: whenever new literature arrives, rerank and extract only logically relevant, non-conflicting, and high-credibility snippets; if multiple consistent snippets exist, raise confidence and consolidate; if conflicting, preserve both lines with annotated conflicts and a meta-claim about discrepancy, marking which is more supported by current evidence<cite id="e93bc512-4">Agent-based scientific QA often lacks explicit reranking; DeepEra bridges by integrating agentic reasoning into reranking to filter misleading evidence</cite>.

5) Novelty- and uncertainty-triggered “assimilation vs accommodation”
- In CL, novelty detection plus uncertainty estimates can gate whether updates are assimilated (coexist with minor changes) or accommodated (major schema/claim changes); methods like incDFM show continual novelty detection integrated into incremental pipelines, while active selection based on uncertainty prioritizes what to learn next and what to keep stable<cite id="490a4a6a-3">Novelty detection and active learning depend on high-quality uncertainty; in CL, uncertainty degrades without continual integration, motivating specialized methods like incDFM</cite><cite id="490a4a6a-2">Entropy/margin/softmax uncertainty selects uncertain samples for labeling and guides both active learning and novelty scoring during continual updates</cite>.
- For assistants: if new evidence is novel but consistent and low-uncertainty, assimilate by updating timestamps, confidence, and summary; if high-uncertainty or inconsistent, trigger accommodation: revise claims, add disclaimers, or create a versioned entry with the new interpretation and a conflict tag<cite id="490a4a6a-3">Quality of uncertainty in CL deteriorates without continual integration, leading to errors that accumulate as new tasks are encountered</cite>.

6) Architecture- and memory-based mitigation to preserve coexistence
- CL techniques—experience replay, regularization, parameter isolation, and network expansion—preserve older knowledge, allowing assistants to maintain older findings as separate branches or read-only summaries while plasticity slots accommodate new results<cite id="0ff96ec3-3">Replay, regularization, parameter isolation, and network expansion are common CL techniques; novelty detection (recognizing new instances) is a strong driver for integrating novelties without supervision</cite>.
- Policy implication: maintain a memory bank of claim–evidence tuples with versioning; use replay-like mechanisms to periodically refresh old claims with new context without overwriting; apply regularization to constrain new updates away from high-confidence old claims unless new evidence strongly contradicts<cite id="0ff96ec3-3">Replay, regularization, and parameter isolation aim to retain old knowledge while acquiring new; few-shot online continual learning emphasizes novelty detection to integrate novelties</cite>.

# Concrete Assistant Patterns That Implement “Overwrite vs Coexist”

- Self-RAG/CRAG/FLARE/SIM-RAG style loops: the assistant emits reflection tokens or explicit “sufficiency/gap” judgments, triggers corrective retrieval when contradictions or gaps are detected, and iteratively refines the answer; this operationalizes “coexist” via incremental revisions and “overwrite” via final, higher-confidence claims after sufficient evidence<cite id="e93bc512-0">Self-RAG enables models to decide when to retrieve and critically evaluate responses; CRAG and FLARE refine answers through iterative retrieval and uncertainty-triggered retrieval</cite><cite id="e93bc512-2">S2G-RAG formalizes sufficiency/gap judging; SIM-RAG and RAG-Critic train critics to accept or continue searching based on evidence and error taxonomies</cite>.
- DeepEra-style evidence reranking: before updating a claim, rerank the union of old and new evidence to filter misleading or irrelevant passages; if reranking resolves conflicts, overwrite the claim with a higher-confidence synthesis; if conflicts persist, preserve both interpretations with confidence bounds and an unresolved flag<cite id="e93bc512-4">DeepEra’s agentic reranking explicitly models logical relevance and evidential support, addressing semantically similar but logically irrelevant passages</cite>.
- Uncertainty- and novelty-gated update policies: compute uncertainty and novelty scores for each claim relative to the new literature; update (overwrite) claims with low novelty and high inconsistency unless uncertainty is low; maintain parallel records (coexist) when novelty is high or uncertainty is moderate, and schedule a future reconciliation meeting a threshold for sufficiency<cite id="490a4a6a-3">Uncertainty-based novelty detection and active learning are interdependent in CL; poor uncertainty leads to error accumulation without continual integration</cite><cite id="490a4a6a-2">Entropy/margin/softmax uncertainty can drive both selection of uncertain samples and scoring for novelty detection to integrate new knowledge</cite>.
- Versioned summaries with stability–plasticity priors: assign time- and impact-based priors (e.g., high-quality venues, recent replications) to new evidence; update confidence and prominence of claims accordingly, but retain older claims as “historical” entries with annotations when new evidence is inconclusive or conflicting<cite id="0ff96ec3-1">AI Scientist systems’ instability hinders integrating findings across periods; maintaining a coherent longitudinal body of knowledge requires mechanisms beyond naive updating</cite><cite id="0ff96ec3-2">Older datasets can suffer greater forgetting under iterative fine-tuning, suggesting time-aware decay and selective preservation</cite>.

# Rules of Thumb for Overwrite vs. Coexistence

- Overwrite when: new literature is (a) novel yet unifies with existing claims via high-confidence, consistent evidence; (b) directly contradicts prior claims, and the contradiction is localized enough to correct the specific claim rather than spawn a parallel version; or (c) reveals a methodological error in prior work, with replicated results supporting the new conclusion<cite id="0ff96ec3-4">Balancing plasticity and stability allows targeted integration of new knowledge without wholesale overwrite of all prior concepts</cite><cite id="e93bc512-1">Retrieval augmentation reduces contradictions by ~30–50%, but residual contradictions often arise from irrelevant or missing evidence, implying targeted corrections when new relevant evidence arrives</cite>.
- Coexist when: new findings are (a) temporally adjacent and increase confidence; (b) partially overlapping but not decisively resolving ambiguity; or (c) irreconcilable with strong uncertainty on both sides; maintain parallel entries with conflict tags, weighted confidence, and a meta-claim that the field has divergent evidence, with a plan to revisit in the future<cite id="0ff96ec3-4">Too much stability prevents learning new concepts; too much plasticity overwrites; CL methods seek the balance through memory, regularization, and architecture</cite><cite id="490a4a6a-4">Detecting “In vs Out,” “In vs Forg,” and “Forg vs Out” shows that confusion grows over stages; methods must distinguish forgotten from in-distribution to avoid indiscriminate overwrite</cite>.
- Safety valves: maintain provenance and uncertainty throughout; if uncertainty rises during integration, revert to coexistence; if uncertainty falls and evidence is consistent, schedule an overwrite with rollback capability; use novelty detection to avoid touching non-overlapping domains and triggering unnecessary overwrite cascades<cite id="490a4a6a-3">Reliable uncertainty is foundational for novelty detection and active learning; uncertainty degrades without continual integration, necessitating mechanisms to avoid poor novelties and misselection</cite>.

# Putting It Together: A Practical Stack for a Scientific Assistant

- Evidence intake: version incoming papers; extract claims; compute initial novelty and relevance using CL novelty detectors and semantic filters<cite id="490a4a6a-3">Novelty detection integrated into continual pipelines (e.g., incDFM) helps distinguish new from old and forgotten, avoiding indiscriminate overwrite</cite>.
- Evidence fusion: apply deep evidence reranking to filter misleading passages; compute uncertainty on each claim relative to new evidence; maintain a memory bank of claim–evidence tuples with versioning and timestamps<cite id="e93bc512-4">DeepEra’s reranking models logical relevance and evidential support to mitigate semantically similar but logically irrelevant evidence</cite><cite id="490a4a6a-2">Entropy/margin/softmax and Bayesian uncertainty can drive both selection and scoring for continual updates and active learning</cite>.
- Decision engine: if novelty is low and consistency is high with uncertainty below threshold → overwrite claim, update confidence, demote older version; if novelty high or uncertainty moderate → coexist with parallel entries, mark as pending reconciliation; if novelty high and inconsistency → create conflict channel and schedule targeted retrieval to resolve; use critics (SIM-RAG/RAG-Critic) to gate acceptance or further search<cite id="e93bc512-2">Critic-guided workflows (SIM-RAG, RAG-Critic) accept answers or continue searching based on error-aware evaluation, enabling targeted correction</cite><cite id="e93bc512-0">Self-RAG and CRAG implement iterative retrieval and self-correction to enhance factual accuracy</cite>.
- Stability safeguards: replay-style refresh of old claims with new context without full retraining; parameter isolation or memory-based ensembles to preserve older findings; schedule periodic reevaluation as uncertainty and consensus evolve<cite id="0ff96ec3-3">Replay, regularization, parameter isolation, and network expansion preserve old knowledge while acquiring new; novelty detection integrates novelties without supervision</cite><cite id="0ff96ec3-2">Iterative fine-tuning can overwrite old knowledge; susceptibility varies by model and dataset, suggesting cautious replay and decay schedules</cite>.

# Caveats and Evaluation

- Overwrite policies risk cascading errors if uncertainty is miscalibrated; continual updating degrades uncertainty quality unless explicitly addressed, so integrate incDFM-style continual novelty detection and uncertainty-aware active learning to avoid blind overwrites<cite id="490a4a6a-3">In CL, uncertainty estimates deteriorate without continual integration, leading to poor novelty detection and sample selection and accumulating errors</cite>.
- Coexistence can bloat knowledge graphs; maintain policies to prune irrelevant or fully absorbed entries and use active retrieval to surface only the most supported or conflicted claims during user queries<cite id="e93bc512-0">Agentic RAG emphasizes iterative retrieval and refinement to avoid absorbing unverifiable or redundant evidence, improving factual accuracy</cite>.
- End-to-end evaluation should measure longitudinal accuracy (consistency with time-evolving literature), contradiction rate before/after update, and user-oriented clarity of conflict disclosures; retrieval-augmented settings show substantial reductions in self-contradictions, but nontrivial residual rates justify cautious overwrite policies and conflict-first coexistence<cite id="e93bc512-1">Retrieval augmentation reduces self-contradictions by ~30–50% but leaves 10–38% remaining with high precision, often from irrelevant or missing evidence</cite>.

Title: Continual Novelty Detection
Snippet: Research in this field is inspired by biological intelligence, however, mammals in general are known for their distinctive ability to discriminate familiar objects from novel objects (Antunes & Biala, 2012;Broadbent et al., 2010). When faced with a novel object, they try to discover and acquire information on the novel object, thus adding it to the set of familiar known objects. Continual learning and novelty detection are essential interconnected components of intelligence yet they are currently studied as independent problems. Moreover, in continual learning, forgetting of some previously learned skills can be unavoidable and a model's knowledge is not only expanding but also shifting, raising the question of how forgotten data will or should be treated by a novelty detection method. 

In this work, we define and formulate the problem of Continual Novelty Detection, which arises when novelty detection methods are applied in a continual learning scenario where the concerned prediction model is continuously updating its existing knowledge. We divide the set of inspected samples into three subsets: (In) samples covering those of previously and recently learned concepts, (Forg) forgotten samples subject to mistaken predictions as a result of continual learning and, finally, the (Out) samples, covering those of yet unseen concepts. Our key goals are to understand (a) the existing novelty detection methods behaviour in this setting; (b) whether novelty detection methods are capable of coping with a dynamic (In) set; (c) how potentially forgotten samples are treated by the novelty detection methods. To this end, we propose a benchmark to evaluate several existing novelty detection methods. 

We note a clear connection between continual learning and novelty detection and insights that novelty detection methods can provide about a continual learner's behaviour and vice versa. We also highlight the need for developing new novelty detection methods that are closely linked to the trained model and the deployed continual learning method. Our contributions are as follows:1) we are the first to investigate the novelty detection problem under the continual learning setting (3); 2) we establish benchmarks for the described continual novelty detection problem and compare different existing methods (4); 3) To stimulate research on this problem, we highlight possible promising directions and propose simple yet effective baselines (A.7).
</snippet>

Title: How Far Are AI Scientists from Changing the World?
Snippet: Despite their remarkable progress, LLMs that serve as the foundation for AI Scientist systems exhibit several intrinsic limitations, including hallucinations, high costs and inefficiencies in knowledge updating, and catastrophic forgetting. These challenges critically constrain the scientific utility and reliability of current AI Scientist systems, making it crucial to address them for the advancement of AI-driven scientific research. 

Hallucination. In scientific research, precision, factual accuracy, and reliability are paramount. However, LLMs are prone to "hallucination", a phenomenon where the model generates plausible-sounding but false or unverifiable content (Huang et al., 2025b, Zhang et al., 2025). This can manifest in several ways: (1) The model may fabricate research findings, experimental data, references, or even entirely non-existent theories, presenting them as factually correct. 

(2) AI-generated citations, data, and formulas are often unreliable or improperly sourced, making it difficult for human researchers to trace and verify the origin and validity Catastrophic Forgetting. Another fundamental challenge is catastrophic forgetting, which is the tendency of neural networks to lose previously acquired information when trained on new data (Kirkpatrick et al., 2017). 

For an AI Scientist, this challenge means that attempts to update the model with new scientific knowledge may inadvertently overwrite or degrade its understanding of existing scientific concepts, methods, and facts. Such instability undermines the system's ability to maintain a comprehensive and coherent body of scientific knowledge over time. As a result, integrating findings across different periods and scientific fields becomes particularly challenging, which in turn impairs the LLM-based AI Scientist systems' capacities to perform longitudinal analyses, connect historical insights with emerging discoveries, and deliver consistent, reliable support for complex scientific explorations.
</snippet>

Title: Benchmarking Large Language Models for Polymer Property Predictions
Snippet: To explore the feasibility of continual learning, referred to in this paper as MT-Seq, we tested a method where models were fine-tuned iteratively to study a hypothetical scenario where additional data or data for new properties become available at a later time. The goal was to evaluate whether a model could retain previously learned knowledge while integrating new information. Two tests were conducted to investigate this. 

In the first test, sequential training was applied to the T g dataset only. However, for T d , GPT's performance remained comparable to the MT and ST configurations, potentially due to overfitting on the T d dataset. Interestingly, GPT-3.5 exhibited an intuitive trend where the oldest dataset (T g ) suffered the greatest forgetting, while information about more recent dataset, (T m ) were retained to a greater degree. In contrast, LLaMA-MT-Seq showed consistent performance degradation across all three datasets, without any clear retention of recent data, further highlighting its susceptibility to the phenomenon known in computer science as 'catastrophic forgetting'. 

These results underscore the limitations of continual learning in LLMs, with both models exhibiting 'catastrophic forgetting' when fine-tuned iteratively on datasets. These findings align with existing literature, where continual fine-tuning has shown to result in similar forgetting behavior [37]. This phenomenon, also known as the palimpsest effect, occurs when newly learned information overwrites previously acquired knowledge [38].
</snippet>

Title: Continual Learning for Autonomous Robots: A Prototype-based Approach
Snippet: Autonomous, interactive, and lifelong learning are features of human intelligence that distinguish it from the machine intelligence of the modern age.Current machine learning methods outperform both humans and hand-crafted algorithm on a given static data set, but fail spectacularly when the key assumptions of the neural network training scheme, e.g., of identically and independently distributed (i.i.d.) data, are violated [1].To address the limitations of static data distribution, Continual Learning (CL) is an emerging topic in AI.The main issue CL aims to address is catastrophic forgetting, the phenomenon that reflects the trade-off between attaining new knowledge while retaining the old knowledge, Fig. 1: Continually Learning Prototypes: overview also known as the plasticity-stability dilemma [2].Replay, regularization, parameter isolation, and network expansion methods have been some of the most common techniques in the CL literature [1], [3].

However, the problem of catastrophic forgetting is not the only challenge that must be addressed to close the gap between today's training of deep neural networks and the more natural learning processes we know from humans and animals.Recently, learning objects from a few labeled samples provided through a non-repeating stream of input has gained attention [4], [5].This setting, formally called fewshot online continual learning (FS-OCL), is a step towards realistic learning for robots.

Yet, FS-OCL is still far from real-world learning scenarios.For instance, human concept learning involves not only a small amount of direct instruction (e.g., parental labeling) but also large amounts of unlabeled experience (e.g., observation of objects without naming them).This unsupervised learning is continual, autonomous, and interactive.A strong driver of this learning process is novelty detection -the ability to recognize an instance as something not seen before [6], [7].On the contrary, a common close-world assumption in deep learning is that all the test instances are from the learned classes.Detecting novel instances alone is not enough, however, as such a system should also integrate these novelties into its knowledge, even without supervision [8].
</snippet>

Title: Out-of-Distribution Detection for Continual Learning: Design Principles and Benchmarking
Snippet: Continual Learning (CL), also known as lifelong learning or incremental learning, is a branch of machine learning that focuses on developing models that can learn continuously from a stream of data over time. The core challenge that CL addresses is the stability-plasticity dilemma. Plasticity refers to a model's ability to acquire and adapt to new information, while stability ensures that previously learned knowledge is preserved. Striking a balance between these two aspects is critical as too much plasticity leads to catastrophic forgetting, i.e., when new learning overwrites past knowledge; whereas too much stability results in an inability to learn new concepts. CL research is typically organized around three main learning settings: a) Task Incremental Learning (TIL), where training happens in sequential batches of tasks and While there exists a vast amount of literature in the field and new methods to curb forgetting are discovered regularly, the diverse landscape of methods often poses a challenge of overlapping categories across literature. To bring coherence to these overlapping perspectives, we group CL into 3 meta-categories: memory-, regularization-, and architecture-based methods. They are formally discussed below.

Title: Uncertainty Quantification in Continual Open-World Learning
Snippet: Methods under Generalized Category Discovery (GCD) [31,48] do address the scenario in which both old and new classes co-occur in the test data. However, they are designed for single-task setups where the entire unlabeled dataset is presented to the model at once for categorization, rather than in a continual, classincremental manner. These solutions are ill-suited for (postdeployment) continual learning as they assume full data availability (labeled and unlabeled) and perform expensive full re-trainings poorly scalable to CL. Similarly, most solutions for novelty or out-of-distribution (OOD) detection [23,28,30,37,50] were developed for and evaluated against a single fixed binary partition of known (old) versus novel classes and not on continual splits. Such conventional OOD models are not designed to continually integrate and learn from the detected novel data. 

Overall, both novelty detection and active learning depend on the availability of reliable, high-quality uncertainty estimates, see figure 1. A variety of uncertainty quantification techniques have been studied: softmax probability and its temperature-scaled variants [23,30]; predictive uncertainty from Bayesian Neural Networks [18]; feature-based Mahalanobis distances [28] and its variants [2]. These methods work well in fixed settings where the model is trained once. However, in CL settings where the model parameters are continually updated, the quality of uncertainty estimates deteriorates as knowledge from novel tasks and classes is incrementally integrated. Such estimates, if used either for novelty detection or for active sample selection, will lead to poor prediction of novelties and/or a poor choice of samples selected for CL. Furthermore, errors tend to accumulate as new tasks are encountered, resulting in progressively poorer performance over time. A recent model, incDFM [42], attempted to address this problem by proposing a solution to continual novelty detection and integrated it into the broader pipeline of unsupervised class incremental learning. However, the number of novel classes introduced at each task was limited to one, so that any detected novelty could then be trivially labeled as belonging to a single novel class.
</snippet>

Title: Continual Novelty Detection
Snippet: We introduce the problem of continual novelty detection, a problem that emerges when novelty detection techniques are deployed in a continual learning scenario. We divide the detection problem into three subproblems, In vs. Out, In vs. Forg and Forg vs. Out. We examine several novelty detection techniques on these sub-problems in various continual learning settings. We show an increase in the detection error of In vs. Out as a result of continual learning. Surprisingly, the most simple ND method, Softmax, works best, yet poorly, in the studied settings opening the door for more sophisticated methods to tackle this challenging problem. When investigating how the Forg set is treated, it appears that as learning stages are carried, the confusion with In set increases. However, unless the Out set is composed of a different dataset, it is extremely hard for current ND methods to discriminate In from Forg. We present baselines improving over Softmax in an attempt to stimulate further research in this problem.
</snippet></tool_output>

Below are continual learning strategies that let a scientific assistant decide when new literature should overwrite versus coexist with prior conclusions. We synthesize mechanisms across continual learning (CL), uncertainty and novelty detection, and retrieval-grounded QA, and map them to concrete policies for updating a scientific narrative.

# Core Problem and Decision Framing

Continual learning systems face a plasticity–stability trade‑off: too much plasticity causes catastrophic forgetting where new learning overwrites old; too much stability prevents learning new findings, leading to irrelevance and contradictions over time<cite id="0ff96ec3-4">Striking a balance between plasticity and stability is critical; too much plasticity leads to catastrophic forgetting where new learning overwrites past knowledge, while too much stability prevents learning new concepts</cite><cite id="0ff96ec3-1">LLMs underpinning AI Scientist systems suffer hallucinations and inefficient knowledge updating with catastrophic forgetting, where updating can overwrite prior concepts and facts</cite><cite id="0ff96ec3-2">Iterative fine-tuning can exhibit “palimpsest” behavior where new data overwrite prior knowledge, demonstrating catastrophic forgetting</cite>. For scientific assistants, the question becomes: when new evidence is (i) novel, (ii) contradicts prior claims, (iii) sufficiently uncertain/conflicted, or (iv) temporally/epistemologically superior, should the agent update (overwrite) or preserve parallel versions (coexist)?

# Algorithmic Building Blocks That Operationalize “Overwrite vs Coexist”

1) Uncertainty-aware updating and selective retraining
- Reliable uncertainty estimates are essential to decide whether current knowledge fits new data; methods like softmax probabilities, entropy/margin, temperature-scaled scores, Bayesian predictive uncertainty, and Mahalanobis distances inform continual novelty detection and active learning updates<cite id="490a4a6a-3">Uncertainty estimation (softmax, entropy/margin/softmax variants; Bayesian neural networks; Mahalanobis distance) is crucial; in CL, uncertainty quality degrades over time without continual integration, leading to poor novelty detection and sample selection unless addressed</cite><cite id="490a4a6a-2">Baselines for continual novelty detection use entropy/margin/softmax uncertainty to select uncertain samples and output scores; uncertainty metrics integrated into continual training updates</cite>. 
- Incorporating continual novelty detection into incremental pipelines (e.g., incDFM) enables the system to distinguish “in-distribution vs novel” and to trigger targeted updates rather than wholesale retraining, reducing overwrite risk for stable findings<cite id="490a4a6a-3">incDFM integrates continual novelty detection into unsupervised class incremental learning, enabling detection and integration of novel data rather than global retraining</cite><cite id="490a4a6a-1">COUQ provides uncertainty for continual novelty detection and active learning, showing utility across sub-tasks</cite>.
- Practical policy: if posterior uncertainty on a claim is below a threshold given new evidence, defer or merge; if uncertainty is high and evidence is consistent, update weights; if evidence is inconsistent, trigger conflict analysis rather than blanket overwrite<cite id="490a4a6a-3">Novelty and active learning depend on reliable uncertainty; poor uncertainty in CL leads to errors accumulating over time, motivating mechanisms that integrate new knowledge without full retraining</cite>.

2) Novelty and out-of-distribution detection at the stream level
- Novelty detection links directly to CL: separating “in” (previously/recently learned), “forgotten” (previously correct now misclassified due to drift), and “out” (novel) supports targeted integration; simple softmax-based detectors can be surprisingly robust, but distinguishing “forgotten” from “in” remains hard without continual integration mechanisms<cite id="0ff96ec3-0">Novelty detection links to CL; samples can be partitioned into In (previously/recently learned), Forged (forgotten/now mispredicted), and Out (novel); methods’ behaviors and errors change under continual updating</cite><cite id="0ff96ec3-4">Novelty detection methods can be grouped and evaluated on continual splits; performance degrades without continual integration</cite><cite id="490a4a6a-4">Continual novelty detection divides into In vs Out, In vs Forg, and Forg vs Out; detection error increases with continual learning, and simple softmax can work best yet poorly depending on settings</cite>.
- Policy implication: classify new literature as novel, redundant, or conflicting; if novel and sufficiently distinct, create a parallel record and schedule a later merge/evaluation; if forgotten/irrelevant, demote or discard; if overlapping and consistent, update confidence and summaries<cite id="0ff96ec3-4">Balancing plasticity and stability lets systems preserve old knowledge while integrating new; methods cluster into memory-, regularization-, and architecture-based families</cite>.

3) Self-correcting RAG pipelines and iterative retrieval
- Agentic RAG introduces iterative retrieval–reflection–refinement cycles for self-correction, enabling models to detect when additional evidence is needed and to revise prior answers; methods like Self-RAG, CRAG, FLARE, ActiveRAG, and RAG-Critic operationalize correction loops and error-aware decision-making over retrieval and generation<cite id="e93bc512-0">Agentic RAG (Self-RAG, CRAG, FLARE, ActiveRAG) iteratively retrieves and refines responses, enabling self-correction and improved factual accuracy in multi-document QA</cite><cite id="e93bc512-2">FLARE triggers retrieval based on generation-time uncertainty; ReSP iterates retrieve–summarize–plan; SIM-RAG and RAG-Critic train critics to accept answers or continue searching based on error taxonomies, enabling targeted correction</cite>.
- Quantitatively, retrieval augmentation reduces self-contradictions by ~30–50% but a notable fraction remains, indicating that contradictions often stem from irrelevant or missing evidence; this motivates policies that overwrite earlier claims when new evidence directly contradicts with high confidence, or coexist with annotations when confidence is moderate<cite id="e93bc512-1">Retrieval augmentation reduces self-contradictions by ~30% (ChatGPT) and ~50% (Llama2-70B) yet 12.7–38.0% of sentences remain contradictory with high precision; contradictions often arise from irrelevant or lacking crucial information</cite>.
- Policy implication: maintain a working answer with provenance and confidence; on new literature, run a quick sufficiency check: if evidence resolves gaps or contradicts with high confidence, update the claim and confidence; if only partially relevant or conflicted, produce a coexisting view with highlighted conflicts and a resolution plan<cite id="e93bc512-2">S2G-RAG formalizes structured sufficiency and gap judging, interleaving retrieval control to accept answers or continue searching based on evidence evaluation</cite>.

4) Evidence reranking for scientific accuracy and conflict mitigation
- Scientific assistants risk absorbing semantically similar yet logically irrelevant passages; deep evidence reranking with agentic reasoning explicitly models logical relevance and evidential support, filtering misleading evidence before fusion into answers<cite id="e93bc512-4">DeepEra introduces an agentic deep evidence reranking agent that models logical relevance and evidential support to address vulnerabilities of surface-level rerankers and the lack of explicit reranking in agent-based scientific QA</cite>.
- Policy implication: whenever new literature arrives, rerank and extract only logically relevant, non-conflicting, and high-credibility snippets; if multiple consistent snippets exist, raise confidence and consolidate; if conflicting, preserve both lines with annotated conflicts and a meta-claim about discrepancy, marking which is more supported by current evidence<cite id="e93bc512-4">Agent-based scientific QA often lacks explicit reranking; DeepEra bridges by integrating agentic reasoning into reranking to filter misleading evidence</cite>.

5) Novelty- and uncertainty-triggered “assimilation vs accommodation”
- In CL, novelty detection plus uncertainty estimates can gate whether updates are assimilated (coexist with minor changes) or accommodated (major schema/claim changes); methods like incDFM show continual novelty detection integrated into incremental pipelines, while active selection based on uncertainty prioritizes what to learn next and what to keep stable<cite id="490a4a6a-3">Novelty detection and active learning depend on high-quality uncertainty; in CL, uncertainty degrades without continual integration, motivating specialized methods like incDFM</cite><cite id="490a4a6a-2">Entropy/margin/softmax uncertainty selects uncertain samples for labeling and guides both active learning and novelty scoring during continual updates</cite>.
- For assistants: if new evidence is novel but consistent and low-uncertainty, assimilate by updating timestamps, confidence, and summary; if high-uncertainty or inconsistent, trigger accommodation: revise claims, add disclaimers, or create a versioned entry with the new interpretation and a conflict tag<cite id="490a4a6a-3">Quality of uncertainty in CL deteriorates without continual integration, leading to errors that accumulate as new tasks are encountered</cite>.

6) Architecture- and memory-based mitigation to preserve coexistence
- CL techniques—experience replay, regularization, parameter isolation, and network expansion—preserve older knowledge, allowing assistants to maintain older findings as separate branches or read-only summaries while plasticity slots accommodate new results<cite id="0ff96ec3-3">Replay, regularization, parameter isolation, and network expansion are common CL techniques; novelty detection (recognizing new instances) is a strong driver for integrating novelties without supervision</cite>.
- Policy implication: maintain a memory bank of claim–evidence tuples with versioning; use replay-like mechanisms to periodically refresh old claims with new context without overwriting; apply regularization to constrain new updates away from high-confidence old claims unless new evidence strongly contradicts<cite id="0ff96ec3-3">Replay, regularization, and parameter isolation aim to retain old knowledge while acquiring new; few-shot online continual learning emphasizes novelty detection to integrate novelties</cite>.

# Concrete Assistant Patterns That Implement “Overwrite vs Coexist”

- Self-RAG/CRAG/FLARE/SIM-RAG style loops: the assistant emits reflection tokens or explicit “sufficiency/gap” judgments, triggers corrective retrieval when contradictions or gaps are detected, and iteratively refines the answer; this operationalizes “coexist” via incremental revisions and “overwrite” via final, higher-confidence claims after sufficient evidence<cite id="e93bc512-0">Self-RAG enables models to decide when to retrieve and critically evaluate responses; CRAG and FLARE refine answers through iterative retrieval and uncertainty-triggered retrieval</cite><cite id="e93bc512-2">S2G-RAG formalizes sufficiency/gap judging; SIM-RAG and RAG-Critic train critics to accept or continue searching based on evidence and error taxonomies</cite>.
- DeepEra-style evidence reranking: before updating a claim, rerank the union of old and new evidence to filter misleading or irrelevant passages; if reranking resolves conflicts, overwrite the claim with a higher-confidence synthesis; if conflicts persist, preserve both interpretations with confidence bounds and an unresolved flag<cite id="e93bc512-4">DeepEra’s agentic reranking explicitly models logical relevance and evidential support, addressing semantically similar but logically irrelevant passages</cite>.
- Uncertainty- and novelty-gated update policies: compute uncertainty and novelty scores for each claim relative to the new literature; update (overwrite) claims with low novelty and high inconsistency unless uncertainty is low; maintain parallel records (coexist) when novelty is high or uncertainty is moderate, and schedule a future reconciliation meeting a threshold for sufficiency<cite id="490a4a6a-3">Uncertainty-based novelty detection and active learning are interdependent in CL; poor uncertainty leads to error accumulation without continual integration</cite><cite id="490a4a6a-2">Entropy/margin/softmax uncertainty can drive both selection of uncertain samples and scoring for novelty detection to integrate new knowledge</cite>.
- Versioned summaries with stability–plasticity priors: assign time- and impact-based priors (e.g., high-quality venues, recent replications) to new evidence; update confidence and prominence of claims accordingly, but retain older claims as “historical” entries with annotations when new evidence is inconclusive or conflicting<cite id="0ff96ec3-1">AI Scientist systems’ instability hinders integrating findings across periods; maintaining a coherent longitudinal body of knowledge requires mechanisms beyond naive updating</cite><cite id="0ff96ec3-2">Older datasets can suffer greater forgetting under iterative fine-tuning, suggesting time-aware decay and selective preservation</cite>.

# Rules of Thumb for Overwrite vs. Coexistence

- Overwrite when: new literature is (a) novel yet unifies with existing claims via high-confidence, consistent evidence; (b) directly contradicts prior claims, and the contradiction is localized enough to correct the specific claim rather than spawn a parallel version; or (c) reveals a methodological error in prior work, with replicated results supporting the new conclusion<cite id="0ff96ec3-4">Balancing plasticity and stability allows targeted integration of new knowledge without wholesale overwrite of all prior concepts</cite><cite id="e93bc512-1">Retrieval augmentation reduces contradictions by ~30–50%, but residual contradictions often arise from irrelevant or missing evidence, implying targeted corrections when new relevant evidence arrives</cite>.
- Coexist when: new findings are (a) temporally adjacent and increase confidence; (b) partially overlapping but not decisively resolving ambiguity; or (c) irreconcilable with strong uncertainty on both sides; maintain parallel entries with conflict tags, weighted confidence, and a meta-claim that the field has divergent evidence, with a plan to revisit in the future<cite id="0ff96ec3-4">Too much stability prevents learning new concepts; too much plasticity overwrites; CL methods seek the balance through memory, regularization, and architecture</cite><cite id="490a4a6a-4">Detecting “In vs Out,” “In vs Forg,” and “Forg vs Out” shows that confusion grows over stages; methods must distinguish forgotten from in-distribution to avoid indiscriminate overwrite</cite>.
- Safety valves: maintain provenance and uncertainty throughout; if uncertainty rises during integration, revert to coexistence; if uncertainty falls and evidence is consistent, schedule an overwrite with rollback capability; use novelty detection to avoid touching non-overlapping domains and triggering unnecessary overwrite cascades<cite id="490a4a6a-3">Reliable uncertainty is foundational for novelty detection and active learning; uncertainty degrades without continual integration, necessitating mechanisms to avoid poor novelties and misselection</cite>.

# Putting It Together: A Practical Stack for a Scientific Assistant

- Evidence intake: version incoming papers; extract claims; compute initial novelty and relevance using CL novelty detectors and semantic filters<cite id="490a4a6a-3">Novelty detection integrated into continual pipelines (e.g., incDFM) helps distinguish new from old and forgotten, avoiding indiscriminate overwrite</cite>.
- Evidence fusion: apply deep evidence reranking to filter misleading passages; compute uncertainty on each claim relative to new evidence; maintain a memory bank of claim–evidence tuples with versioning and timestamps<cite id="e93bc512-4">DeepEra’s reranking models logical relevance and evidential support to mitigate semantically similar but logically irrelevant evidence</cite><cite id="490a4a6a-2">Entropy/margin/softmax and Bayesian uncertainty can drive both selection and scoring for continual updates and active learning</cite>.
- Decision engine: if novelty is low and consistency is high with uncertainty below threshold → overwrite claim, update confidence, demote older version; if novelty high or uncertainty moderate → coexist with parallel entries, mark as pending reconciliation; if novelty high and inconsistency → create conflict channel and schedule targeted retrieval to resolve; use critics (SIM-RAG/RAG-Critic) to gate acceptance or further search<cite id="e93bc512-2">Critic-guided workflows (SIM-RAG, RAG-Critic) accept answers or continue searching based on error-aware evaluation, enabling targeted correction</cite><cite id="e93bc512-0">Self-RAG and CRAG implement iterative retrieval and self-correction to enhance factual accuracy</cite>.
- Stability safeguards: replay-style refresh of old claims with new context without full retraining; parameter isolation or memory-based ensembles to preserve older findings; schedule periodic reevaluation as uncertainty and consensus evolve<cite id="0ff96ec3-3">Replay, regularization, parameter isolation, and network expansion preserve old knowledge while acquiring new; novelty detection integrates novelties without supervision</cite><cite id="0ff96ec3-2">Iterative fine-tuning can overwrite old knowledge; susceptibility varies by model and dataset, suggesting cautious replay and decay schedules</cite>.

# Caveats and Evaluation

- Overwrite policies risk cascading errors if uncertainty is miscalibrated; continual updating degrades uncertainty quality unless explicitly addressed, so integrate incDFM-style continual novelty detection and uncertainty-aware active learning to avoid blind overwrites<cite id="490a4a6a-3">In CL, uncertainty estimates deteriorate without continual integration, leading to poor novelty detection and sample selection and accumulating errors</cite>.
- Coexistence can bloat knowledge graphs; maintain policies to prune irrelevant or fully absorbed entries and use active retrieval to surface only the most supported or conflicted claims during user queries<cite id="e93bc512-0">Agentic RAG emphasizes iterative retrieval and refinement to avoid absorbing unverifiable or redundant evidence, improving factual accuracy</cite>.
- End-to-end evaluation should measure longitudinal accuracy (consistency with time-evolving literature), contradiction rate before/after update, and user-oriented clarity of conflict disclosures; retrieval-augmented settings show substantial reductions in self-contradictions, but nontrivial residual rates justify cautious overwrite policies and conflict-first coexistence<cite id="e93bc512-1">Retrieval augmentation reduces self-contradictions by ~30–50% but leaves 10–38% remaining with high precision, often from irrelevant or missing evidence</cite>.

In summary, scientific assistants can operationalize “overwrite vs coexist” by combining continual novelty detection, calibrated uncertainty, agentic self-correction with iterative retrieval, deep evidence reranking, and versioned memory; use thresholds on novelty and inconsistency to decide whether to consolidate or preserve parallel, annotated findings, and apply replay/isolation techniques to protect prior knowledge while integrating new literature in a plasticity–stability balanced manner<cite id="0ff96ec3-4">CL addresses stability–plasticity via memory-, regularization-, and architecture-based methods</cite><cite id="490a4a6a-3">Uncertainty-based novelty detection and active learning are foundational; incDFM integrates continual novelty detection to avoid full retraining</cite><cite id="e93bc512-0">Self-RAG, CRAG, FLARE, and ActiveRAG implement iterative retrieval and self-correction to enhance factual accuracy</cite><cite id="e93bc512-2">S2G-RAG, SIM-RAG, and RAG-Critic provide structured sufficiency/gap judging and error-aware correction</cite><cite id="e93bc512-4">DeepEra’s agentic evidence reranking explicitly models logical relevance to filter misleading passages in scientific QA</cite><cite id="0ff96ec3-1">AI Scientist systems must mitigate hallucinations and inefficient knowledge updating and catastrophic forgetting to reliably integrate new literature</cite><cite id="0ff96ec3-2">Iterative fine-tuning may overwrite prior knowledge (palimpsest effect), underscoring the need for careful integration policies</cite>.</answer>

Title: Continual Novelty Detection
Snippet: Research in this field is inspired by biological intelligence, however, mammals in general are known for their distinctive ability to discriminate familiar objects from novel objects (Antunes & Biala, 2012;Broadbent et al., 2010). When faced with a novel object, they try to discover and acquire information on the novel object, thus adding it to the set of familiar known objects. Continual learning and novelty detection are essential interconnected components of intelligence yet they are currently studied as independent problems. Moreover, in continual learning, forgetting of some previously learned skills can be unavoidable and a model's knowledge is not only expanding but also shifting, raising the question of how forgotten data will or should be treated by a novelty detection method. 

In this work, we define and formulate the problem of Continual Novelty Detection, which arises when novelty detection methods are applied in a continual learning scenario where the concerned prediction model is continuously updating its existing knowledge. We divide the set of inspected samples into three subsets: (In) samples covering those of previously and recently learned concepts, (Forg) forgotten samples subject to mistaken predictions as a result of continual learning and, finally, the (Out) samples, covering those of yet unseen concepts. Our key goals are to understand (a) the existing novelty detection methods behaviour in this setting; (b) whether novelty detection methods are capable of coping with a dynamic (In) set; (c) how potentially forgotten samples are treated by the novelty detection methods. To this end, we propose a benchmark to evaluate several existing novelty detection methods. 

We note a clear connection between continual learning and novelty detection and insights that novelty detection methods can provide about a continual learner's behaviour and vice versa. We also highlight the need for developing new novelty detection methods that are closely linked to the trained model and the deployed continual learning method. Our contributions are as follows:1) we are the first to investigate the novelty detection problem under the continual learning setting (3); 2) we establish benchmarks for the described continual novelty detection problem and compare different existing methods (4); 3) To stimulate research on this problem, we highlight possible promising directions and propose simple yet effective baselines (A.7).

Title: How Far Are AI Scientists from Changing the World?
Snippet: Despite their remarkable progress, LLMs that serve as the foundation for AI Scientist systems exhibit several intrinsic limitations, including hallucinations, high costs and inefficiencies in knowledge updating, and catastrophic forgetting. These challenges critically constrain the scientific utility and reliability of current AI Scientist systems, making it crucial to address them for the advancement of AI-driven scientific research. 

Hallucination. In scientific research, precision, factual accuracy, and reliability are paramount. However, LLMs are prone to "hallucination", a phenomenon where the model generates plausible-sounding but false or unverifiable content (Huang et al., 2025b, Zhang et al., 2025). This can manifest in several ways: (1) The model may fabricate research findings, experimental data, references, or even entirely non-existent theories, presenting them as factually correct. 

(2) AI-generated citations, data, and formulas are often unreliable or improperly sourced, making it difficult for human researchers to trace and verify the origin and validity Catastrophic Forgetting. Another fundamental challenge is catastrophic forgetting, which is the tendency of neural networks to lose previously acquired information when trained on new data (Kirkpatrick et al., 2017). 

For an AI Scientist, this challenge means that attempts to update the model with new scientific knowledge may inadvertently overwrite or degrade its understanding of existing scientific concepts, methods, and facts. Such instability undermines the system's ability to maintain a comprehensive and coherent body of scientific knowledge over time. snippet.text:
Research in this field is inspired by biological intelligence, however, mammals in general are known for their distinctive ability to discriminate familiar objects from novel objects (Antunes & Biala, 2012;Broadbent et al., 2010). When faced with a novel object, they try to discover and acquire information on the novel object, thus adding it to the set of familiar known objects. Continual learning and novelty detection are essential interconnected components of intelligence yet they are currently studied as independent problems. Moreover, in continual learning, forgetting of some previously learned skills can be unavoidable and a model's knowledge is not only expanding but also shifting, raising the question of how forgotten data will or should be treated by a novelty detection method. 

In this work, we define and formulate the problem of Continual Novelty Detection, which arises when novelty detection methods are applied in a continual learning scenario where the concerned prediction model is continuously updating its existing knowledge. We divide the set of inspected samples into three subsets: (In) samples covering those of previously and recently learned concepts, (Forg) forgotten samples subject to mistaken predictions as a result of continual learning and, finally, the (Out) samples, covering those of yet unseen concepts. Our key goals are to understand (a) the existing novelty detection methods behaviour in this setting; (b) whether novelty detection methods are capable of coping with a dynamic (In) set; (c) how potentially forgotten samples are treated by the novelty detection methods. To this end, we propose a benchmark to evaluate several existing novelty detection methods. 

We note a clear connection between continual learning and novelty detection and insights that novelty detection methods can provide about a continual learner's behaviour and vice versa. We also highlight the need for developing new novelty detection methods that are closely linked to the trained model and the deployed continual learning method. Our contributions are as follows:1) we are the first to investigate the novelty detection problem under the continual learning setting (3); 2) we establish benchmarks for the described continual novelty detection problem and compare different existing methods (4); 3) To stimulate research on this problem, we highlight possible promising directions and propose simple yet effective baselines (A.7).

snippet.text:
Despite their remarkable progress, LLMs that serve as the foundation for AI Scientist systems exhibit several intrinsic limitations, including hallucinations, high costs and inefficiencies in knowledge updating, and catastrophic forgetting. These challenges critically constrain the scientific utility and reliability of current AI Scientist systems, making it crucial to address them for the advancement of AI-driven scientific research. 

Hallucination. In scientific research, precision, factual accuracy, and reliability are paramount. However, LLMs are prone to "hallucination", a phenomenon where the model generates plausible-sounding but false or unverifiable content (Huang et al., 2025b, Zhang et al., 2025). This can manifest in several ways: (1) The model may fabricate research findings, experimental data, references, or even entirely non-existent theories, presenting them as factually correct. 

(2) AI-generated citations, data, and formulas are often unreliable or improperly sourced, making it difficult for human researchers to trace and verify the origin and validity Catastrophic Forgetting. Another fundamental challenge is catastrophic forgetting, which is the tendency of neural networks to lose previously acquired information when trained on new data (Kirkpatrick et al., 2017). 

For an AI Scientist, this challenge means that attempts to update the model with new scientific knowledge may inadvertently overwrite or degrade its understanding of existing scientific concepts, methods, and facts. Such instability undermines the system's ability to maintain a comprehensive and coherent body of scientific knowledge over time. As a result, integrating findings across different periods and scientific fields becomes particularly challenging, which in turn impairs the LLM-based AI Scientist systems' capacities to perform longitudinal analyses, connect historical insights with emerging discoveries, and deliver consistent, reliable support for complex scientific explorations.

Title: Uncertainty Quantification in Continual Open-World Learning
Snippet: We apply our uncertainty estimation method COUQ to a general open-world continual learning setting defined in §2. We demonstrate its utility and effectiveness on the following sub-tasks therein: (1) Continual Novelty Detection, results in §4.2; (2) Continual Active Learning, results in §4.3.

Title: Uncertainty Quantification in Continual Open-World Learning
Snippet: (A) Baselines for only Continual Novelty Detection (CND): 

(1) incDFM [42], a method that includes an updatable continual novelty detector, but assumes single class novelties (see §2.2); (2) DFM [33], a precursor of incDFM originally proposed for non-continual novelty detection; (B) Baselines for only Continual Open-World Novelty Learning (CONL): (3) CCIC [9] a semi-supervised CL model that adapts MixMatch [8] to the CL setting; (4) GBCL, a few-shot continual active learning approach [5]; (C) Baselines used for both CND and CONL: (5) (ERvariants) Semi-supervised baselines built upon the CL technique of Experience Replay [12,43] based on [49] for active continual learning. For these, uncertainty metrics such as (5.1) Entropy, (5.2) Margin, (5.3) Softmax are used to actively select the most uncertain samples for labeling which will be used in continual training updates. The same uncertainty metrics are then used to output scores for evaluation; (6) For further comparison, we introduce additional baselines built upon the previous item ER-variants but using the corresponding uncertainty quantification (e.g. Entropy, Margin or Softmax) to iteratively pseudolabel the most confident samples during the inner loop akin to our approach.

Title: Uncertainty Quantification in Continual Open-World Learning
Snippet: Methods under Generalized Category Discovery (GCD) [31,48] do address the scenario in which both old and new classes co-occur in the test data. However, they are designed for single-task setups where the entire unlabeled dataset is presented to the model at once for categorization, rather than in a continual, classincremental manner. These solutions are ill-suited for (postdeployment) continual learning as they assume full data availability (labeled and unlabeled) and perform expensive full re-trainings poorly scalable to CL. Similarly, most solutions for novelty or out-of-distribution (OOD) detection [23,28,30,37,50] were developed for and evaluated against a single fixed binary partition of known (old) versus novel classes and not on continual splits. Such conventional OOD models are not designed to continually integrate and learn from the detected novel data. 

Overall, both novelty detection and active learning depend on the availability of reliable, high-quality uncertainty estimates, see figure 1. A variety of uncertainty quantification techniques have been studied: softmax probability and its temperature-scaled variants [23,30]; predictive uncertainty from Bayesian Neural Networks [18]; feature-based Mahalanobis distances [28] and its variants [2]. These methods work well in fixed settings where the model is trained once. However, in CL settings where the model parameters are continually updated, the quality of uncertainty estimates deteriorates as knowledge from novel tasks and classes is incrementally integrated. Such estimates, if used either for novelty detection or for active sample selection, will lead to poor prediction of novelties and/or a poor choice of samples selected for CL. Furthermore, errors tend to accumulate as new tasks are encountered, resulting in progressively poorer performance over time. A recent model, incDFM [42], attempted to address this problem by proposing a solution to continual novelty detection and integrated it into the broader pipeline of unsupervised class incremental learning. However, the number of novel classes introduced at each task was limited to one, so that any detected novelty could then be trivially labeled as belonging to a single novel class.

Title: Continual Novelty Detection
Snippet: We introduce the problem of continual novelty detection, a problem that emerges when novelty detection techniques are deployed in a continual learning scenario. We divide the detection problem into three subproblems, In vs. Out, In vs. Forg and Forg vs. Out. We examine several novelty detection techniques on these sub-problems in various continual learning settings. We show an increase in the detection error of In vs. Out as a result of continual learning. Surprisingly, the most simple ND method, Softmax, works best, yet poorly, in the studied settings opening the door for more sophisticated methods to tackle this challenging problem. When investigating how the Forg set is treated, it appears that as learning stages are carried, the confusion with In set increases. However, unless the Out set is composed of a different dataset, it is extremely hard for current ND methods to discriminate In from Forg. We present baselines improving over Softmax in an attempt to stimulate further research in this problem.

snippet.text:
Methods under Generalized Category Discovery (GCD) [31,48] do address the scenario in which both old and new classes co-occur in the test data. However, they are designed for single-task setups where the entire unlabeled dataset is presented to the model at once for categorization, rather than in a continual, classincremental manner. These solutions are ill-suited for (postdeployment) continual learning as they assume full data availability (labeled and unlabeled) and perform expensive full re-trainings poorly scalable to CL. Similarly, most solutions for novelty or out-of-distribution (OOD) detection [23,28,30,37,50] were developed for and evaluated against a single fixed binary partition of known (old) versus novel classes and not on continual splits. Such conventional OOD models are not designed to continually integrate and learn from the detected novel data. 

Overall, both novelty detection and active learning depend on the availability of reliable, high-quality uncertainty estimates, see figure 1. A variety of uncertainty quantification techniques have been studied: softmax probability and its temperature-scaled variants [23,30]; predictive uncertainty from Bayesian Neural Networks [18]; feature-based Mahalanobis distances [28] and its variants [2]. These methods work well in fixed settings where the model is trained once. However, in CL settings where the model parameters are continually updated, the quality of uncertainty estimates deteriorates as knowledge from novel tasks and classes is incrementally integrated. Such estimates, if used either for novelty detection or for active sample selection, will lead to poor prediction of novelties and/or a poor choice of samples selected for CL. Furthermore, errors tend to accumulate as new tasks are encountered, resulting in progressively poorer performance over time. A recent model, incDFM [42], attempted to address this problem by proposing a solution to continual novelty detection and integrated it into the broader pipeline of unsupervised class incremental learning. However, the number of novel classes introduced at each task was limited to one, so that any detected novelty could then be trivially labeled as belonging to a single novel class.

snippet.text: We introduce the problem of continual novelty detection, a problem that emerges when novelty detection techniques are deployed in a continual learning scenario. We divide the detection problem into three subproblems, In vs. Out, In vs. Forg and Forg vs. Out. We examine several novelty detection techniques on these sub-problems in various continual learning settings. We show an increase in the detection error of In vs. Out as a result of continual learning. Surprisingly, the most simple ND method, Softmax, works best, yet poorly, in the studied settings opening the door for more sophisticated methods to tackle this challenging problem. When investigating how the Forg set is treated, it appears that as learning stages are carried, the confusion with In set increases. However, unless the Out set is composed of a different dataset, it is extremely hard for current ND methods to discriminate In from Forg. We present baselines improving over Softmax in an attempt to stimulate further research in this problem.

documents.title: Continual Novelty Detection
documents.snippet:
Research in this field is inspired by biological intelligence, however, mammals in general are known for their distinctive ability to discriminate familiar objects from novel objects (Antunes & Biala, 2012;Broadbent et al., 2010). When faced with a novel object, they try to discover and acquire information on the novel object, thus adding it to the set of familiar known objects. Continual learning and novelty detection are essential interconnected components of intelligence yet they are currently studied as independent problems. Moreover, in continual learning, forgetting of some previously learned skills can be unavoidable and a model's knowledge is not only expanding but also shifting, raising the question of how forgotten data will or should be treated by a novelty detection method. 

In this work, we define and formulate the problem of Continual Novelty Detection, which arises when novelty detection methods are applied in a continual learning scenario where the concerned prediction model is continuously updating its existing knowledge. We divide the set of inspected samples into three subsets: (In) samples covering those of previously and recently learned concepts, (Forg) forgotten samples subject to mistaken predictions as a result of continual learning and, finally, the (Out) samples, covering those of yet unseen concepts. Our key goals are to understand (a) the existing novelty detection methods behaviour in this setting; (b) whether novelty detection methods are capable of coping with a dynamic (In) set; (c) how potentially forgotten samples are treated by the novelty detection methods. To this end, we propose a benchmark to evaluate several existing novelty detection methods. 

We note a clear connection between continual learning and novelty detection and insights that novelty detection methods can provide about a continual learner's behaviour and vice versa. We also highlight the need for developing new novelty detection methods that are closely linked to the trained model and the deployed continual learning method. Our contributions are as follows:1) we are the first to investigate the novelty detection problem under the continual learning setting (3); 2) we establish benchmarks for the described continual novelty detection problem and compare different existing methods (4); 3) To stimulate research on this problem, we highlight possible promising directions and propose simple yet effective baselines (A.7).

Title: HiQA: A Hierarchical Contextual Augmentation RAG for Multi-Documents QA
Snippet: Agentic strategies in RAG involve iterative cycles of retrieval, reflection, and refinement, enabling models to engage in self-correction and enhance factual accuracy, particularly in multi-document question answering scenarios. Self-RAG [21] introduces a self-supervised mechanism where the model decides when to retrieve additional information and critically evaluates its own responses, leading to improvements in open-domain question answering. Similarly, CRAG [22] employs corrective retrieval augmented generation, focusing on iterative refinement of responses through multiple retrieval and generation steps. Further advancements include FLARE [17], which predicts future content to guide retrieval, and ActiveRAG [23], which incorporates autonomous knowledge assimilation and accommodation through a multi-agent framework. These approaches demonstrate that agentic strategies, by facilitating continuous interaction between retrieval and generation processes, significantly enhance the performance of RAG systems in complex QA tasks.

Title: Self-contradictory Hallucinations of Large Language Models: Evaluation, Detection and Mitigation
Snippet: We adapt our approach to question answering as described at the end of Section 5. We focus on 1.5K randomly sampled questions from PopQA (Mallen et al., 2023). We perform experiments in two settings, vanilla generation, and retrieval augmentation, where generation and detection are provided with adaptively retrieved text snippets as proposed by Mallen et al. (2023). We use ChatGPT as aLM and the default temperatures (see the end of Section 6.1). To compute the precision of our detection method, we manually annotate all sentence pairs that are predicted to be contradictory. 

The results for the two evaluated gLM, ChatGPT and Llama2-70B-Chat, are presented in Table 5. Even though self-contradictions decrease in the retrieval augmented setting by around 30% in ChatGPT and almost 50% in Llama2-70B-Chat, a significant amount of self-contradictions (12.7% to 38.0%) is detected in all settings with high precision (74.2% to 83.8%). This implies that even with retrieval augmentation, at least 10.6% of ChatGPT and 16.0% of Llama2-70B-Chat generated answers contain self-contradictions. A qualitative analysis shows that self-contradictions often arise when the retrieved knowledge is irrelevant to the posed question or lacks the crucial information for a correct answer. This reaffirms our claim that our method serves as a valuable complement to retrieval-based methods.

Title: S2G-RAG: Structured Sufficiency and Gap Judging for Iterative Retrieval-Augmented QA
Snippet: We compare S2G-RAG against representative baselines spanning single-round RAG and multi-round retrieval control. NaiveGen (Jin et al., 2025) answers without retrieval. Standard RAG (Jin et al., 2025) performs a single retrieval using the original question and generates an answer conditioned on the retrieved documents. IR-CoT (Trivedi et al., 2023) interleaves retrieval with intermediate reasoning signals that serve as retrieval cues. FLARE (Jiang et al., 2023) triggers retrieval based on generation-time uncertainty signals. ReSP (Jiang et al., 2025) iterates retrievesummarize-plan to manage multi-turn evidence accumulation. Self-RAG (Asai et al., 2024) finetunes a generator to emit explicit reflection tokens that govern retrieval behavior. SIM-RAG (Yang et al., 2025) trains a lightweight critic that, at each round, evaluates the reasoner's provisional answer and accompanying rationale against the currently retrieved context and decides whether to accept the answer or continue searching. RAG-Critic (Dong et al., 2025) introduces an error-aware critic that is trained with a hierarchical error taxonomy and provides fine-grained feedback about potential RAG failures, which is then used to trigger targeted correction workflows in an agentic RAG pipeline.

Title: UR2: Unify RAG and Reasoning through Reinforcement Learning
Snippet: This approach consolidates the multi-agent architecture into a unified model with structured prompting, ensuring consistent evaluation across all baselines while preserving the essential reasoning patterns. 

Self-Ask with Retrieval-Augmented Generation: Our implementation follows the Self-Ask framework's (Press et al., 2023) question decomposition strategy, employing batch retrieval from the local KILT corpus to enhance efficiency. The system maintains the characteristic "Follow up:" and "Intermediate answer:" reasoning chain format, with stopping criteria incorporating both semantic completion detection and a maximum of 10 follow-up questions. When decomposition challenges arise, the framework seamlessly transitions to standard RAG, ensuring robust performance across diverse question types. 

RAT (Retrieval-Augmented Thought): We adapt RAT (Wang et al., 2024b) for unified evaluation across reasoning and QA tasks. The framework retains the core principle of knowledgeenhanced reasoning while operating at the paragraph level rather than the sentence level, with corresponding modifications to the prompting strategy. This design choice maintains consistency with our evaluation infrastructure while capturing RAT's fundamental insight of augmenting reasoning processes with relevant external knowledge. 

All advanced RAG methods operate within a standardized retrieval infrastructure: documents are retrieved from the 100-word segmented KILT Wikipedia corpus (29M documents in total). For GPT-family models, we use top-k=10 retrieval. Due to model limitations, LLaMA and Qwen variants use top-k=5. For summarization or other auxiliary operations beyond reasoning, each model performs the processing itself rather than relying on GPT-4.1, ensuring consistency with its own capabilities.

Title: DeepEra: A Deep Evidence Reranking Agent for Scientific Retrieval-Augmented Generated Question Answering
Snippet: Our work relates to three research lines: scientific question answering, retrieval augmented generation with reranking, and agentic scientific QA. Although diverse rerankers ranging from dense and sparse to listwise and LLM-based methods have been proposed (NetEase Youdao, 2023;Chen et al., 2024;Jina AI, 2024), most rely on surfacelevel semantic similarity and remain vulnerable to semantically similar but logically irrelevant passages. Meanwhile, agent based scientific QA enables multi step retrieval and reasoning but typically lacks explicit reranking to filter misleading evidence. (Lála et al., 2023;Zhang et al., 2025a) Our Deep Evidence Reranking Agent bridges these directions by introducing agentic reasoning into reranking, explicitly modeling logical relevance and evidential support. A detailed review of related work is provided in Appendix 6.1.
