attempts.answer:
Overview and challenge
Scientific assistants that learn continually from the literature must avoid incorporating claims from retracted papers or irreproducible studies. In practice, off‑the‑shelf generative tools often fail to detect retractions or warn users, so assistants need explicit, auditable mechanisms to verify the integrity of newly integrated findings and to prefer robust, reproducible evidence over time. <cite id="52294d5f-3">Generative AI tools commonly used for literature searches and evidence synthesis do not consistently recognize retracted articles; retractions are frequently included in topic overviews without warning and systems often fail when explicitly asked about retraction status</cite>. This motivates assistants to integrate provenance, citation-graph, and quality signals into retrieval and synthesis pipelines and to make these checks part of the decision process and user-facing artifacts.

Signals and sources for verifying retractions and integrity
Modern assistants can verify retractions and research integrity by leveraging specialized databases, publisher/metadata signals, and citation-graph monitoring. <cite id="1ff18395-0">Retraction status in biomedical AI literature can be systematically identified by querying PubMed with a “retracted publication” filter, enabling assistants to surface and exclude retracted items during evidence gathering</cite>. <cite id="1ff18395-3">Retraction Watch is widely used to enumerate and track reasons for retractions and has been integrated to understand the status of retracted publications in AI</cite>. <cite id="e873da4c-1">PubMed explicitly marks retractions and this retraction list can be used as a machine-readable starting point; CrossMark by CrossRef provides automated notifications of retractions though coverage depends on publisher participation</cite>. <cite id="e873da4c-1">Automated systems can monitor bibliographic updates to build and maintain citation networks for retracted papers, enabling detection of direct and chain citations to retractions</cite>.

Beyond retractions, assistants can evaluate irreproducibility and robustness by assessing methodological quality and conflict patterns in the retrieved evidence. <cite id="e873da4c-1">Because a paper is retracted as a whole even if some passages remain valid, passage search engines should expose the retracted status of the citing paper to avoid propagating invalidated content; automated provenance requires structured publisher signals</cite>. <cite id="52294d5f-4">Tools like Scite leverage a large publication database and analyze how each cited paper relates to a topic, distinguishing supportive vs. conflicting evidence and surfacing citations so users can audit claims and assess evidence quality</cite>. <cite id="52294d5f-4">Elicit builds an evidence table with document-grounded claims and quotes, enabling provenance capture, traceability to original studies, and user‑driven inclusion/exclusion criteria with deduplication</cite>.

Evidence selection and auditing mechanisms used by assistants
Contemporary evidence-grounded assistants enforce provenance and auditability at retrieval and answer composition time to reduce hallucinations and make new findings verifiable. <cite id="e873da4c-2">Hybrid retrieval plus reranking improves answer correctness and citation precision, and introducing final citation filtering reduces hallucination substantially; a clean “evidence chain” that enforces only selected-family citations yields 92.23% correctness with 7.77% hallucination and higher citation precision, making answers easier to audit</cite>. <cite id="e873da4c-3">Private assistants should maintain domain lexicons and use them as reranking features, but must enforce final citation filtering; evidence-chain scoring aggregates support deterministically and filters final citations to a compact, coherent chain that is slower than hybrid retrieval but keeps hallucination to a minimum</cite>. <cite id="e873da4c-2">Operationalizing this, assistants can log per-query correctness, citation precision, hallucination flags, latency, token budgets, and top chunk identifiers, enabling reproducible evaluation and traceability to raw artifacts</cite>.

Provenance needs to capture trajectories, not just cited sources. <cite id="e873da4c-0">In agentic graph-based RAG, accurate answers depend on more than the final cited entities: traversal context, neighborhood structure, and visited-but-uncited entities shape discovery, selection, and interpretation; thus, citation faithfulness requires trajectory-level provenance beyond final citations</cite>. Assistive systems can combine these trajectory-level and source-level provenance records with explicit retraction flags to verify that newly integrated findings are not invalidated by retractions or propagated conflicts.

Quality and robustness checks to flag irreproducible findings
Assistants can integrate quality and robustness signals that surface irreproducible or low‑robustness claims during continual updates. <cite id="e873da4c-4">In regulatory/clinical reasoning, lexical retrieval (BM25) outperforms dense baselines and ReContriever on aligning retrieved top‑k passages to gold provenance for both factual and multi‑hop tasks, indicating that section-style phrasing and exact matches are critical; this supports assistants that enforce strict lexical overlap and section-level provenance checks to reduce spurious inclusions</cite>. <cite id="52294d5f-4">Conflict-aware citation scoring (support vs. conflicting evidence) and source-grounded extraction (quotes, evidence tables) help users judge whether new findings are broadly corroborated or contested, reducing reliance on single‑study claims</cite>.

Dynamic monitoring and human oversight to maintain integrity
Because retraction and quality information changes over time, continual learning assistants need dynamic verification and human-in-the-loop safeguards. <cite id="e873da4c-1">Automated monitors can continuously scan incoming bibliographic updates to track citations to retracted papers, enabling assistants to flag downstream documents and statements that reference invalidated work</cite>. <cite id="52294d5f-4">Oversight patterns include provenance capture, scope locking with explicit inclusion/exclusion criteria, and deduplication to ensure that new integrations adhere to the user’s evidence standards and question scope</cite>. <cite id="52294d5f-3">Given that general AI tools often fail to detect retractions or communicate retraction status, research-oriented assistants should explicitly interrogate retrieved items for retraction notices, cross-check against Retraction Watch and PubMed/CrossMark signals, and present warnings and alternatives when conflicts are found</cite>.

Practical workflow for verification in a continual learning assistant
Putting these mechanisms together, a scientific assistant can verify newly integrated findings with the following steps:
1) Source-level integrity checks: cross-reference each candidate study and its passages against retraction databases (Retraction Watch), structured publisher/metadata signals (PubMed retraction marks, CrossMark), and internal cache of retracted DOIs/PMIDs; surface explicit warnings when a paper is retracted or under correction. <cite id="1ff18395-0">PubMed provides a retracted-publication filter that can be queried to enumerate and exclude retracted items</cite> <cite id="e873da4c-1">PubMed explicitly marks retractions and CrossMark can automate notifications if publishers participate</cite> <cite id="1ff18395-3">Retraction Watch is used to enumerate and understand retraction status and reasons for retractions</cite>.
2) Citation-graph and trajectory provenance: build a retrieval provenance graph capturing traversal, visited-but-uncited nodes, and neighborhood context; verify that claims are supported by stable, non-conflicting clusters rather than single sources. <cite id="e873da4c-0">Trajectory-level provenance is necessary because visited-but-uncited entities and neighborhood structure influence evidence selection and interpretation</cite>.
3) Evidence-family filtering and audit trails: enforce final citation filtering to a coherent evidence chain from the correct domain family; present per-citation snippets and section-level quotes to allow auditing and to reduce hallucination and contamination from mixed or invalid sources. <cite id="e873da4c-2">Final citation filtering and evidence chains reduce hallucination and make answers easier to verify; they yield high correctness with low hallucination and clean citation sets</cite> <cite id="e873da4c-3">Enforcing final citation filtering and deterministic support aggregation focuses the answer path and reduces uncertainty before action</cite>.
4) Conflict and robustness scoring: score each claim’s support vs. conflicting evidence and prefer convergent findings; require multi-paragraph, section-level matches to gold provenance in retrieval to avoid spurious support from mismatched embeddings. <cite id="e873da4c-4">Lexical overlap and section-style phrasing drive accurate citation alignment to gold provenance, outperforming dense and multi-hop baselines, supporting strict lexical/provenance checks</cite> <cite id="52294d5f-4">Scite-style supportive/conflicting labeling and source-grounded outputs enable users to assess evidence quality and trace claims</cite>.
5) Dynamic monitoring and human-in-the-loop: continuously update retraction and quality indices; apply temporal decay and novelty heuristics; and allow users to lock inclusion/exclusion criteria and review flagged items (e.g., newly added low-robustness clusters or items referencing retracted work). <cite id="e873da4c-1">Citation networks for retracted papers can be maintained by monitoring bibliographic updates, flagging direct and chain citations</cite> <cite id="52294d5f-4">Oversight includes provenance capture, scope lock, and deduplication to maintain integrity during continual updates</cite>.

What to expect from current tools and remaining limitations
Early research-oriented assistants and general AI tools reveal both capabilities and shortcomings. <cite id="52294d5f-4">Elicit and Scite provide strong provenance and conflict-aware features: Elicit builds document-grounded evidence tables; Scite distinguishes supportive vs. conflicting evidence and surfaces citations for verification</cite>. <cite id="52294d5f-3">However, widely used GenAI tools frequently include retracted articles in overviews without warning and struggle to correctly report retraction status, underscoring that assistants must not rely on default behavior and must add explicit retraction and provenance checks</cite>. Coverage and machine-readability of retraction signals also vary across publishers and metadata layers. <cite id="e873da4c-1">While PubMed and CrossMark provide structured signals, CrossMark’s coverage is incomplete and Retraction Watch, though increasingly formalized, must be queried and integrated to automate checks</cite>. Finally, assistants face the challenge that retraction does not necessarily invalidate all content; tools should distinguish whole-paper retractions from potentially salvageable passages and present users with the right granularity for decision-making. <cite id="e873da4c-1">A passage may remain valid even when its parent paper is retracted, so passage-level QA engines should expose retraction status of the citing paper and avoid propagating invalidated content</cite>.

Summary
Continual learning methods for scientific assistants verify newly integrated findings by combining structured integrity checks (retraction databases and publisher signals), provenance-aware retrieval (trajectory and citation provenance), evidence-family filtering with auditable chains, conflict/robustness scoring, and dynamic human oversight. <cite id="52294d5f-3">Because general AI tools often fail to detect retractions on their own</cite>, assistants must explicitly cross-check retraction status, surface source-level evidence for audit, and prefer convergent, non-conflicting, and machine-verifiable support. <cite id="52294d5f-4">Existing tools like Elicit and Scite already implement these principles through provenance capture, conflict-aware citation scoring, and source-grounded outputs</cite>, and <cite id="e873da4c-0">trajectory-level provenance</cite> and <cite id="e873da4c-2">evidence-chain filtering</cite> further reduce hallucinations and make verification practical at scale. <cite id="1ff18395-0">Querying PubMed’s retracted publication filter</cite> and <cite id="e873da4c-1">leveraging PubMed/CrossMark retraction marks</cite> provide concrete, implementable signals, while <cite id="e873da4c-1">automated monitoring of citation networks</cite> enables continual detection of downstream contamination. The end result is an auditable, risk-aware pipeline where newly integrated findings are traceable to primary sources, flagged if tied to retractions or weak evidence, and prioritized by robustness over time. <cite id="52294d5f-3">These steps are necessary because, absent such mechanisms, assistants risk incorporating retracted or irreproducible studies and misleading users</cite>.

Title: Continual Pre-Training Mitigates Forgetting in Language and Vision
Snippet: We provide strong empirical evidence supporting the hypothesis that the continual pre-training scenario is less impacted by catastrophic forgetting than the traditional one. In particular, we found the unsupervised pre-training objective to be the common factor for the resistance to forgetting in the proposed environments. Our result adds to the evidences discussed in Section 2 for the robustness of unsupervised and self-supervised protocols with respect to catastrophic forgetting. Our evaluation offers similar conclusions for the novel continual pre-training scenario. 

Continual pre-training improves performance on the downstream task without forgetting on FC datasets. We verified that continual pre-training positively impacts on the performance on the downstream scientific abstracts classification task. That is, we observed that acquiring domain knowledge on scientific abstracts helps when solving the classification task (on heldout data). Appendix B.2 shows that continual pre-training on 5 experiences improves the downstream classification performance (Table 11). Performance is improved also with one step of pre-training on the entire scientific abstracts dataset. As discussed in Appendix B.2, while the improvement is relatively small, we were able to achieve it by using a smaller number of samples with respect to the common pre-training datasets (e.g. Wikipedia): this points to the fact that continual pre-training does not necessarily need enormous datasets to actually be beneficial (a very useful aspect for continual learning). 

In terms of catastrophic forgetting on the FC dataset after continual pre-training, we show that, quite surprisingly, both RoBERTa (Table 2 and 3) and BERT (Table 4) achieves almost zero forgetting, reaching an accuracy comparable to the one originally obtained by the model before continual pre-training. This happens both for sentiment analysis and QNLI. Moreover, a single epoch of gradient descent is sufficient to retain most of the original performance, showing the quick adaptation capabilities of the pre-trained models. Notably, the additional pretraining steps on domain-specific texts along with the expansion of the RoBERTa vocabulary does not worsen the effects of catastrophic forgetting. We conducted a broader empirical assessment on a diverse set of NLP tasks by using the SentEval benchmark. Figure 2 shows the downstream performance of BERT and RoBERTa after the entire continual pre-training stream.
</snippet>

Title: Performance of AI Tools in Citing Retracted Literature : Content Analysis
Snippet: Abstract Background Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools are increasingly used in scientific research to support literature searches, evidence synthesis, and manuscript preparation. While these systems promise substantial efficiency gains, concerns have emerged regarding their reliability, particularly their tendency to cite inaccurate, fabricated, or retracted literature. The unrecognized inclusion of retracted studies poses a serious risk to research integrity and evidence-based decision-making. Whether commonly used GenAI tools can reliably detect, exclude, or transparently communicate the retraction status of scientific publications remains unclear. Objective This study aimed to evaluate the ability of freely available GenAI tools to correctly handle retracted scientific articles during literature searches. Primary and secondary outcomes focused on accuracy, reliability, and consistency in recognizing retracted literature. Methods In this pragmatic trial, nine widely used free-access GenAI tools (ChatGPT 4, ChatGPT 5, Claude, Gemini, Perplexity, Microsoft Copilot, SciSpace, ScienceOS, and Consensus) were evaluated. Each tool was asked five predefined, standardized questions addressing topic overview, article identification, article summarization, and explicit assessment of retraction status. Overall, 15 retracted articles (the 10 most cited and 5 most recently retracted as of May 23, 2025) were selected from the Retraction Watch database. All questions were repeated twice to assess intratool consistency. Responses were independently rated as correct or incorrect by 2 researchers. Descriptive statistics summarized performance, and comparisons between general-purpose and research-focused AI tools were conducted using descriptive statistics. Interreviewer agreement was assessed using Cohen kappa coefficient. Results None of the evaluated AI tools consistently handled retracted articles correctly. No model achieved perfect accuracy across all question sets. ChatGPT 5 performed best, defined by the primary outcome of achieving fully correct responses to all five predefined tasks (5/5) for the highest number of retracted articles, correctly answering all five questions for 8 of 15 articles (53.3%). Research-focused tools (SciSpace, ScienceOS, and Consensus) failed to produce a single fully correct response set. Retracted articles were frequently included in topic overviews without warning, with error rates exceeding 40% in several tools. When specifically asked about retraction status, most systems failed to provide correct or complete information. OpenEvidence only

Snippet: Software using the Mendeley application programming interface (API) was written to search for the presence of records of retracted articles in the personal libraries of Mendeley users.Mendeley [30] is a popular bibliographic tool that helps scholars manage references, create bibliographies, and share papers with other Mendeley users.While there are other bibliographic management tools used by scholars (EndNote, RefWorks, Zotero, among others), at the time of this study, Mendeley was the only product A study of retracted articles that permitted the development of such an interface to their data set.While we do not consider the behaviors of Mendeley users to be necessarily generalizable to the behaviors of all bibliographic database users, Mendeley does provide us with a novel window into the private libraries held by scholars.The source code, documentation, and implementation information can be found at https://www.github.com/fireisbo/retr/.

The Mendeley interface was designed to operate in batch mode using a search strategy that relied upon title keyword matches, PubMed identification numbers (PMIDs), and digital object identifiers (DOIs).Eliminating case and common punctuation, the algorithm first performed a title keyword search, saving a list of possible matches, and then attempted to verify the results with a PMID or DOI, if available.A positive match was returned with a Mendeley uniform resource locator (URL) and the number of users with the same record-these are defined by Mendeley as ''readers.''If multiple versions of the same record were located, the search algorithm combined and reported the total number of Mendeley readers.The relationship between public accessibility of retracted articles and their frequency in Mendeley libraries was tested by logistic regression.

Title: Performance of AI Tools in Citing Retracted Literature : Content Analysis
Snippet: This study was designed as a pragmatic evaluation using freely accessible artificial intelligence tools (AI) for literature screening and summarization of articles with five predefined questions to assess how retracted articles are handled. The trial was registered during the data acquisition phase in the Open Science Framework (osf.io) [14]. 

The predefined questions were designed to outline a pathway for investigating a new topic of interest: providing an overview based on the article's keywords, identifying the most important research articles related to the defined topic, and summarizing the retracted article. The final two questions were directly aimed at the retraction status of the respective article. Each response was scored as correct (1) or incorrect (0). We used AI tools specifically designed for scientific work (Consensus Version July 2025, SciSpace Version 1.5.1, ScienceOS Version July 2025, OpenEvidence Version July 2025) as well as generic AI tools (ChatGPT Version 4 and 5, Microsoft Copilot Version 3.0, Gemini Version 2.5, Perplexity AI Version July 2025, Claude AI Version 3.5). Title: Why Neighborhoods Matter: Traversal Context and Provenance in Agentic GraphRAG
Snippet: This paper examined whether final citations in Agentic GraphRAG are sufficient to explain the evidence basis of generated answers. Our findings suggest that they are not. While cited entities often play a necessary role and removing them substantially changes answers and reduces accuracy, the experiments also show that accurate answering depends on more than the entities ultimately cited. Graph traversal, neighborhood structure, and visited-but-uncited entities can all influence how the agent discovers, selects, and interprets evidence. 

The results show that citation faithfulness in Agentic GraphRAG requires a broader notion of provenance. A citation set may correctly identify supporting evidence, yet still omit parts of the retrieval trajectory that were relevant to producing the answer. Therefore, evaluating citations only by checking whether the cited sources support the answer, or whether they were visited by the agent, is insufficient. Faithful citation mechanisms should also account for the graph context and retrieval path that shape the final response. 

Overall, our results indicate that provenance in agentic graph-based retrieval should be treated as a trajectory-level property rather than only a final-output property.
</snippet>

Title: Propagation of errors in citation networks: a study involving the entire citation network of a widely cited paper published in, and later retracted from, the journal Nature
Snippet: See also [54] for a discussion on search engines and retractions. 

Finding out about a retraction becomes even more difficult when we do not look for entire articles but for passages instead. Modern information retrieval research investigates so-called passage retrieval, the retrieval of relevant passages rather than entire articles ( [55], ch. 13). A paper is always retracted as a whole even though parts of it may be unaffected by the reasons for retraction. To be useful for practising scientists, a passage retrieval search engine will have to incorporate provisions for retrieving the retracted status of the paper from which the passage stems. To enable search engines to do this, publishers will have to make the status known in a structured way readable by a computer programme. 

The very least that can be done is keeping track of retractions. The Retraction Watch blog does invaluable service here but it is not yet available for automated methods. Recently, the blog announced it had received a grant to set up a database of retractions [56]. PubMed explicitly marks retractions. If this is done in a machinereadable way, PubMed's retraction list is a good starting point for a database of retractions. Also, the commercial service CrossMark by CrossRef promises to keep its users informed of retractions [57]. CrossMark relies on the voluntary participation of publishers, and although the current list of participating publishers is impressive, it is by no means complete. We feel that journal publishers should have done this long ago and for free because they publish both the original articles and their retractions. 

With or without a database of retractions, it is feasible to automatically construct a citation network for a retracted paper. After all, any citation network is a subgraph of the graph defined by the citation relations identified by Scopus, Web of Science or Google Scholar. The programme can be written such that it continually monitors bibliographic descriptions added to the database to keep the network up-to-date. It would be interesting to find out the extent to which the published literature is citing retracted papers either directly or through a citation chain.

Overview and challenge
Scientific assistants that learn continually from the literature must avoid incorporating claims from retracted papers or irreproducible studies. In practice, off‑the‑shelf generative tools often fail to detect retractions or warn users, so assistants need explicit, auditable mechanisms to verify the integrity of newly integrated findings and to prefer robust, reproducible evidence over time. <cite id="52294d5f-3">Generative AI tools commonly used for literature searches and evidence synthesis do not consistently recognize retracted articles; retractions are frequently included in topic overviews without warning and systems often fail when explicitly asked about retraction status</cite>. This motivates assistants to integrate provenance, citation-graph, and quality signals into retrieval and synthesis pipelines and to make these checks part of the decision process and user-facing artifacts.

Signals and sources for verifying retractions and integrity
Modern assistants can verify retractions and research integrity by leveraging specialized databases, publisher/metadata signals, and citation-graph monitoring. <cite id="1ff18395-0">Retraction status in biomedical AI literature can be systematically identified by querying PubMed with a “retracted publication” filter, enabling assistants to surface and exclude retracted items during evidence gathering</cite>. <cite id="1ff18395-3">Retraction Watch is widely used to enumerate and track reasons for retractions and has been integrated to understand the status of retracted publications in AI</cite>. <cite id="e873da4c-1">PubMed explicitly marks retractions and this retraction list can be used as a machine-readable starting point; CrossMark by CrossRef provides automated notifications of retractions though coverage depends on publisher participation</cite>. <cite id="e873da4c-1">Automated systems can monitor bibliographic updates to build and maintain citation networks for retracted papers, enabling detection of direct and chain citations to retractions</cite>.

Beyond retractions, assistants can evaluate irreproducibility and robustness by assessing methodological quality and conflict patterns in the retrieved evidence. <cite id="e873da4c-1">Because a paper is retracted as a whole even if some passages remain valid, passage search engines should expose the retracted status of the citing paper to avoid propagating invalidated content; automated provenance requires structured publisher signals</cite>. <cite id="52294d5f-4">Tools like Scite leverage a large publication database and analyze how each cited paper relates to a topic, distinguishing supportive vs. conflicting evidence and surfacing citations so users can audit claims and assess evidence quality</cite>. <cite id="52294d5f-4">Elicit builds an evidence table with document-grounded claims and quotes, enabling provenance capture, traceability to original studies, and user‑driven inclusion/exclusion criteria with deduplication</cite>.

Evidence selection and auditing mechanisms used by assistants
Contemporary evidence-grounded assistants enforce provenance and auditability at retrieval and answer composition time to reduce hallucinations and make new findings verifiable. <cite id="e873da4c-2">Hybrid retrieval plus reranking improves answer correctness and citation precision, and introducing final citation filtering reduces hallucination substantially; a clean “evidence chain” that enforces only selected-family citations yields 92.23% correctness with 7.77% hallucination and higher citation precision, making answers easier to audit</cite>. <cite id="e873da4c-3">Private assistants should maintain domain lexicons and use them as reranking features, but must enforce final citation filtering; evidence-chain scoring aggregates support deterministically and filters final citations to a compact, coherent chain that is slower than hybrid retrieval but keeps hallucination to a minimum</cite>. <cite id="e873da4c-2">Operationalizing this, assistants can log per-query correctness, citation precision, hallucination flags, latency, token budgets, and top chunk identifiers, enabling reproducible evaluation and traceability to raw artifacts</cite>.

Provenance needs to capture trajectories, not just cited sources. <cite id="e873da4c-0">In agentic graph-based RAG, accurate answers depend on more than the final cited entities: traversal context, neighborhood structure, and visited-but-uncited entities shape discovery, selection, and interpretation; thus, citation faithfulness requires trajectory-level provenance beyond final citations</cite>. Assistive systems can combine these trajectory-level and source-level provenance records with explicit retraction flags to verify that newly integrated findings are not invalidated by retractions or propagated conflicts.

Quality and robustness checks to flag irreproducible findings
Assistants can integrate quality and robustness signals that surface irreproducible or low‑robustness claims during continual updates. <cite id="e873da4c-4">In regulatory/clinical reasoning, lexical retrieval (BM25) outperforms dense baselines and ReContriever on aligning retrieved top‑k passages to gold provenance for both factual and multi‑hop tasks, indicating that section-style phrasing and exact matches are critical; this supports assistants that enforce strict lexical overlap and section-level provenance checks to reduce spurious inclusions</cite>. <cite id="52294d5f-4">Conflict-aware citation scoring (support vs. conflicting evidence) and source-grounded extraction (quotes, evidence tables) help users judge whether new findings are broadly corroborated or contested, reducing reliance on single‑study claims</cite>.

Dynamic monitoring and human oversight to maintain integrity
Because retraction and quality information changes over time, continual learning assistants need dynamic verification and human-in-the-loop safeguards. <cite id="e873da4c-1">Automated monitors can continuously scan incoming bibliographic updates to track citations to retracted papers, enabling assistants to flag downstream documents and statements that reference invalidated work</cite>. <cite id="52294d5f-4">Oversight patterns include provenance capture, scope locking with explicit inclusion/exclusion criteria, and deduplication to ensure that new integrations adhere to the user’s evidence standards and question scope</cite>. <cite id="52294d5f-3">Given that general AI tools often fail to detect retractions or communicate retraction status, research-oriented assistants should explicitly interrogate retrieved items for retraction notices, cross-check against Retraction Watch and PubMed/CrossMark signals, and present warnings and alternatives when conflicts are found</cite>.

Practical workflow for verification in a continual learning assistant
Putting these mechanisms together, a scientific assistant can verify newly integrated findings with the following steps:
1) Source-level integrity checks: cross-reference each candidate study and its passages against retraction databases (Retraction Watch), structured publisher/metadata signals (PubMed retraction marks, CrossMark), and internal cache of retracted DOIs/PMIDs; surface explicit warnings when a paper is retracted or under correction. <cite id="1ff18395-0">PubMed provides a retracted-publication filter that can be queried to enumerate and exclude retracted items</cite> <cite id="e873da4c-1">PubMed explicitly marks retractions and CrossMark can automate notifications if publishers participate</cite> <cite id="1ff18395-3">Retraction Watch is used to enumerate and understand retraction status and reasons for retractions</cite>.
2) Citation-graph and trajectory provenance: build a retrieval provenance graph capturing traversal, visited-but-uncited nodes, and neighborhood context; verify that claims are supported by stable, non-conflicting clusters rather than single sources. <cite id="e873da4c-0">Trajectory-level provenance is necessary because visited-but-uncited entities and neighborhood structure influence evidence selection and interpretation</cite>.
3) Evidence-family filtering and audit trails: enforce final citation filtering to a coherent evidence chain from the correct domain family; present per-citation snippets and section-level quotes to allow auditing and to reduce hallucination and contamination from mixed or invalid sources. <cite id="e873da4c-2">Final citation filtering and evidence chains reduce hallucination and make answers easier to verify; they yield high correctness with low hallucination and clean citation sets</cite> <cite id="e873da4c-3">Enforcing final citation filtering and deterministic support aggregation focuses the answer path and reduces uncertainty before action</cite>.
4) Conflict and robustness scoring: score each claim’s support vs. conflicting evidence and prefer convergent findings; require multi-paragraph, section-level matches to gold provenance in retrieval to avoid spurious support from mismatched embeddings. <cite id="e873da4c-4">Lexical overlap and section-style phrasing drive accurate citation alignment to gold provenance, outperforming dense and multi-hop baselines, supporting strict lexical/provenance checks</cite> <cite id="52294d5f-4">Scite-style supportive/conflicting labeling and source-grounded outputs enable users to assess evidence quality and trace claims</cite>.
5) Dynamic monitoring and human-in-the-loop: continuously update retraction and quality indices; apply temporal decay and novelty heuristics; and allow users to lock inclusion/exclusion criteria and review flagged items (e.g., newly added low-robustness clusters or items referencing retracted work). <cite id="e873da4c-1">Citation networks for retracted papers can be maintained by monitoring bibliographic updates, flagging direct and chain citations</cite> <cite id="52294d5f-4">Oversight includes provenance capture, scope lock, and deduplication to maintain integrity during continual updates</cite>.

What to expect from current tools and remaining limitations
Early research-oriented assistants and general AI tools reveal both capabilities and shortcomings. <cite id="52294d5f-4">Elicit and Scite provide strong provenance and conflict-aware features: Elicit builds document-grounded evidence tables; Scite distinguishes supportive vs. conflicting evidence and surfaces citations for verification</cite>. <cite id="52294d5f-3">However, widely used GenAI tools frequently include retracted articles in overviews without warning and struggle to correctly report retraction status, underscoring that assistants must not rely on default behavior and must add explicit retraction and provenance checks</cite>. Coverage and machine-readability of retraction signals also vary across publishers and metadata layers. <cite id="e873da4c-1">While PubMed and CrossMark provide structured signals, CrossMark’s coverage is incomplete and Retraction Watch, though increasingly formalized, must be queried and integrated to automate checks</cite>. Finally, assistants face the challenge that retraction does not necessarily invalidate all content; tools should distinguish whole-paper retractions from potentially salvageable passages and present users with the right granularity for decision-making. <cite id="e873da4c-1">A passage may remain valid even when its parent paper is retracted, so passage-level QA engines should expose retraction status of the citing paper and avoid propagating invalidated content</cite>.

Summary
Continual learning methods for scientific assistants verify newly integrated findings by combining structured integrity checks (retraction databases and publisher signals), provenance-aware retrieval (trajectory and citation provenance), evidence-family filtering with auditable chains, conflict/robustness scoring, and dynamic human oversight. <cite id="52294d5f-3">Because general AI tools often fail to detect retractions on their own</cite>, assistants must explicitly cross-check retraction status, surface source-level evidence for audit, and prefer convergent, non-conflicting, and machine-verifiable support. <cite id="52294d5f-4">Existing tools like Elicit and Scite already implement these principles through provenance capture, conflict-aware citation scoring, and source-grounded outputs</cite>, and <cite id="e873da4c-0">trajectory-level provenance</cite> and <cite id="e873da4c-2">evidence-chain filtering</cite> further reduce hallucinations and make verification practical at scale. <cite id="1ff18395-0">Querying PubMed’s retracted publication filter</cite> and <cite id="e873da4c-1">leveraging PubMed/CrossMark retraction marks</cite> provide concrete, implementable signals, while <cite id="e873da4c-1">automated monitoring of citation networks</cite> enables continual detection of downstream contamination. The end result is an auditable, risk-aware pipeline where newly integrated findings are traceable to primary sources, flagged if tied to retractions or weak evidence, and prioritized by robustness over time. <cite id="52294d5f-3">These steps are necessary because, absent such mechanisms, assistants risk incorporating retracted or irreproducible studies and misleading users</cite>.
</answer>

Title: Continual Pre-Training Mitigates Forgetting in Language and Vision
Snippet: We provide strong empirical evidence supporting the hypothesis that the continual pre-training scenario is less impacted by catastrophic forgetting than the traditional one. In particular, we found the unsupervised pre-training objective to be the common factor for the resistance to forgetting in the proposed environments. Our result adds to the evidences discussed in Section 2 for the robustness of unsupervised and self-supervised protocols with respect to catastrophic forgetting. Our evaluation offers similar conclusions for the novel continual pre-training scenario. 

Continual pre-training improves performance on the downstream task without forgetting on FC datasets. We verified that continual pre-training positively impacts on the performance on the downstream scientific abstracts classification task. That is, we observed that acquiring domain knowledge on scientific abstracts helps when solving the classification task (on heldout data). Appendix B.2 shows that continual pre-training on 5 experiences improves the downstream classification performance (Table 11). Performance is improved also with one step of pre-training on the entire scientific abstracts dataset. As discussed in Appendix B.2, while the improvement is relatively small, we were able to achieve it by using a smaller number of samples with respect to the common pre-training datasets (e.g. Wikipedia): this points to the fact that continual pre-training does not necessarily need enormous datasets to actually be beneficial (a very useful aspect for continual learning). 

In terms of catastrophic forgetting on the FC dataset after continual pre-training, we show that, quite surprisingly, both RoBERTa (Table 2 and 3) and BERT (Table 4) achieves almost zero forgetting, reaching an accuracy comparable to the one originally obtained by the model before continual pre-training. This happens both for sentiment analysis and QNLI. Moreover, a single epoch of gradient descent is sufficient to retain most of the original performance, showing the quick adaptation capabilities of the pre-trained models. Notably, the additional pretraining steps on domain-specific texts along with the expansion of the RoBERTa vocabulary does not worsen the effects of catastrophic forgetting. We conducted a broader empirical assessment on a diverse set of NLP tasks by using the SentEval benchmark. Figure 2 shows the downstream performance of BERT and RoBERTa after the entire continual pre-training stream.

Title: Performance of AI Tools in Citing Retracted Literature : Content Analysis
Snippet: Abstract Background Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools are increasingly used in scientific research to support literature searches, evidence synthesis, and manuscript preparation. While these systems promise substantial efficiency gains, concerns have emerged regarding their reliability, particularly their tendency to cite inaccurate, fabricated, or retracted literature. The unrecognized inclusion of retracted studies poses a serious risk to research integrity and evidence-based decision-making. Whether commonly used GenAI tools can reliably detect, exclude, or transparently communicate the retraction status of scientific publications remains unclear. Objective This study aimed to evaluate the ability of freely available GenAI tools to correctly handle retracted scientific articles during literature searches. Primary and secondary outcomes focused on accuracy, reliability, and consistency in recognizing retracted literature. Methods In this pragmatic trial, nine widely used free-access GenAI tools (ChatGPT 4, ChatGPT 5, Claude, Gemini, Perplexity, Microsoft Copilot, SciSpace, ScienceOS, and Consensus) were evaluated. Each tool was asked five predefined, standardized questions addressing topic overview, article identification, article summarization, and explicit assessment of retraction status. Overall, 15 retracted articles (the 10 most cited and 5 most recently retracted as of May 23, 2025) were selected from the Retraction Watch database. All questions were repeated twice to assess intratool consistency. Responses were independently rated as correct or incorrect by 2 researchers. Descriptive statistics summarized performance, and comparisons between general-purpose and research-focused AI tools were conducted using descriptive statistics. Interreviewer agreement was assessed using Cohen kappa coefficient. Results None of the evaluated AI tools consistently handled retracted articles correctly. No model achieved perfect accuracy across all question sets. ChatGPT 5 performed best, defined by the primary outcome of achieving fully correct responses to all five predefined tasks (5/5) for the highest number of retracted articles, correctly answering all five questions for 8 of 15 articles (53.3%). Research-focused tools (SciSpace, ScienceOS, and Consensus) failed to produce a single fully correct response set. Retracted articles were frequently included in topic overviews without warning, with error rates exceeding 40% in several tools. When specifically asked about retraction status, most systems failed to provide correct or complete information. OpenEvidence only

snippet.text:
We provide strong empirical evidence supporting the hypothesis that the continual pre-training scenario is less impacted by catastrophic forgetting than the traditional one. In particular, we found the unsupervised pre-training objective to be the common factor for the resistance to forgetting in the proposed environments. Our result adds to the evidences discussed in Section 2 for the robustness of unsupervised and self-supervised protocols with respect to catastrophic forgetting. Our evaluation offers similar conclusions for the novel continual pre-training scenario. 

Continual pre-training improves performance on the downstream task without forgetting on FC datasets. We verified that continual pre-training positively impacts on the performance on the downstream scientific abstracts classification task. That is, we observed that acquiring domain knowledge on scientific abstracts helps when solving the classification task (on heldout data). Appendix B.2 shows that continual pre-training on 5 experiences improves the downstream classification performance (Table 11). Performance is improved also with one step of pre-training on the entire scientific abstracts dataset. As discussed in Appendix B.2, while the improvement is relatively small, we were able to achieve it by using a smaller number of samples with respect to the common pre-training datasets (e.g. Wikipedia): this points to the fact that continual pre-training does not necessarily need enormous datasets to actually be beneficial (a very useful aspect for continual learning). 

In terms of catastrophic forgetting on the FC dataset after continual pre-training, we show that, quite surprisingly, both RoBERTa (Table 2 and 3) and BERT (Table 4) achieves almost zero forgetting, reaching an accuracy comparable to the one originally obtained by the model before continual pre-training. This happens both for sentiment analysis and QNLI. Moreover, a single epoch of gradient descent is sufficient to retain most of the original performance, showing the quick adaptation capabilities of the pre-trained models. Notably, the additional pretraining steps on domain-specific texts along with the expansion of the RoBERTa vocabulary does not worsen the effects of catastrophic forgetting. We conducted a broader empirical assessment on a diverse set of NLP tasks by using the SentEval benchmark. Figure 2 shows the downstream performance of BERT and RoBERTa after the entire continual pre-training stream.

snippet.text: Abstract Background Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools are increasingly used in scientific research to support literature searches, evidence synthesis, and manuscript preparation. While these systems promise substantial efficiency gains, concerns have emerged regarding their reliability, particularly their tendency to cite inaccurate, fabricated, or retracted literature. The unrecognized inclusion of retracted studies poses a serious risk to research integrity and evidence-based decision-making. Whether commonly used GenAI tools can reliably detect, exclude, or transparently communicate the retraction status of scientific publications remains unclear. Objective This study aimed to evaluate the ability of freely available GenAI tools to correctly handle retracted scientific articles during literature searches. Primary and secondary outcomes focused on accuracy, reliability, and consistency in recognizing retracted literature. Methods In this pragmatic trial, nine widely used free-access GenAI tools (ChatGPT 4, ChatGPT 5, Claude, Gemini, Perplexity, Microsoft Copilot, SciSpace, ScienceOS, and Consensus) were evaluated. Each tool was asked five predefined, standardized questions addressing topic overview, article identification, article summarization, and explicit assessment of retraction status. Overall, 15 retracted articles (the 10 most cited and 5 most recently retracted as of May 23, 2025) were selected from the Retraction Watch database. All questions were repeated twice to assess intratool consistency. Responses were independently rated as correct or incorrect by 2 researchers. Descriptive statistics summarized performance, and comparisons between general-purpose and research-focused AI tools were conducted using descriptive statistics. Interreviewer agreement was assessed using Cohen kappa coefficient. Results None of the evaluated AI tools consistently handled retracted articles correctly. No model achieved perfect accuracy across all question sets. ChatGPT 5 performed best, defined by the primary outcome of achieving fully correct responses to all five predefined tasks (5/5) for the highest number of retracted articles, correctly answering all five questions for 8 of 15 articles (53.3%). Research-focused tools (SciSpace, ScienceOS, and Consensus) failed to produce a single fully correct response set. Retracted articles were frequently included in topic overviews without warning, with error rates exceeding 40% in several tools. When specifically asked about retraction status, most systems failed to provide correct or complete information. OpenEvidence only

Snippet: This descriptive cross-sectional investigation systematically discovered and assessed retracted publications related to AI without time limitations. Snippet: Software using the Mendeley application programming interface (API) was written to search for the presence of records of retracted articles in the personal libraries of Mendeley users.Mendeley [30] is a popular bibliographic tool that helps scholars manage references, create bibliographies, and share papers with other Mendeley users.While there are other bibliographic management tools used by scholars (EndNote, RefWorks, Zotero, among others), at the time of this study, Mendeley was the only product A study of retracted articles that permitted the development of such an interface to their data set.While we do not consider the behaviors of Mendeley users to be necessarily generalizable to the behaviors of all bibliographic database users, Mendeley does provide us with a novel window into the private libraries held by scholars.The source code, documentation, and implementation information can be found at https://www.github.com/fireisbo/retr/.

The Mendeley interface was designed to operate in batch mode using a search strategy that relied upon title keyword matches, PubMed identification numbers (PMIDs), and digital object identifiers (DOIs).Eliminating case and common punctuation, the algorithm first performed a title keyword search, saving a list of possible matches, and then attempted to verify the results with a PMID or DOI, if available.A positive match was returned with a Mendeley uniform resource locator (URL) and the number of users with the same record-these are defined by Mendeley as ''readers.''If multiple versions of the same record were located, the search algorithm combined and reported the total number of Mendeley readers.The relationship between public accessibility of retracted articles and their frequency in Mendeley libraries was tested by logistic regression.

Title: Why Neighborhoods Matter: Traversal Context and Provenance in Agentic GraphRAG
Snippet: This paper examined whether final citations in Agentic GraphRAG are sufficient to explain the evidence basis of generated answers. Our findings suggest that they are not. While cited entities often play a necessary role and removing them substantially changes answers and reduces accuracy, the experiments also show that accurate answering depends on more than the entities ultimately cited. Graph traversal, neighborhood structure, and visited-but-uncited entities can all influence how the agent discovers, selects, and interprets evidence. 

The results show that citation faithfulness in Agentic GraphRAG requires a broader notion of provenance. A citation set may correctly identify supporting evidence, yet still omit parts of the retrieval trajectory that were relevant to producing the answer. Therefore, evaluating citations only by checking whether the cited sources support the answer, or whether they were visited by the agent, is insufficient. Faithful citation mechanisms should also account for the graph context and retrieval path that shape the final response. 

Overall, our results indicate that provenance in agentic graph-based retrieval should be treated as a trajectory-level property rather than only a final-output property.

Title: Propagation of errors in citation networks: a study involving the entire citation network of a widely cited paper published in, and later retracted from, the journal Nature
Snippet: See also [54] for a discussion on search engines and retractions.

paper.title: Why Neighborhoods Matter: Traversal Context and Provenance in Agentic GraphRAG

openAccessInfo.disclaimer: Notice: This snippet is extracted from the open access paper or abstract available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.15109, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. Please go to the source to verify the license and copyright information for your use.

snippet.text:
This paper examined whether final citations in Agentic GraphRAG are sufficient to explain the evidence basis of generated answers. Our findings suggest that they are not. While cited entities often play a necessary role and removing them substantially changes answers and reduces accuracy, the experiments also show that accurate answering depends on more than the entities ultimately cited. Graph traversal, neighborhood structure, and visited-but-uncited entities can all influence how the agent discovers, selects, and interprets evidence. 

The results show that citation faithfulness in Agentic GraphRAG requires a broader notion of provenance. A citation set may correctly identify supporting evidence, yet still omit parts of the retrieval trajectory that were relevant to producing the answer. Therefore, evaluating citations only by checking whether the cited sources support the answer, or whether they were visited by the agent, is insufficient. Faithful citation mechanisms should also account for the graph context and retrieval path that shape the final response. 

Overall, our results indicate that provenance in agentic graph-based retrieval should be treated as a trajectory-level property rather than only a final-output property.
